A decade of denoising turned noise into worlds: diffusion models 2015 → 2026

Background: LDM sample · Rombach et al., 2021
Yikai Wang
Hi everyone, I'm Yikai Wang, a postdoctoral researcher at Meta in London, where I work on training video generative models. In this talk, I'll walk through eleven years of diffusion models, from the first diffusion paper in 2015 to today's video and world models. The title itself is generated the way a diffusion model generates: start from Gaussian noise and denoise iteratively.
The arc · 2020 → 2025

From a slow image generator to the generative engine of foundation models

One recipe all along: learn to remove noise at every noise level, then generate by denoising pure noise.

Here is the story in short. In 2020, diffusion was a slow image generator. By 2022 it turned text into images on a gaming graphics card, by 2024 it made minute-long videos, and by 2025 it generated interactive worlds in real time.
Eleven years on one line

From 1000 steps to real-time worlds

Five quiet years, then everything at once: most milestones land between 2020 and 2025.

Here are the milestones on one timeline, in four lanes: methods, image systems, video and worlds, and the fusion of diffusion with language models and reinforcement learning. After the first paper in 2015, things stay quiet for about five years, and then almost everything arrives between 2020 and 2025. The large dots are the papers the short version of this talk covers, and the smaller ones appear only in this full version.

Primer

Diffusion in one picture:
learn to denoise, then denoise noise

forward noising ε-prediction score SDE vs ODE guidance ε / x₀ / v conditioning design choices
I will first introduce the background and definition of diffusion. Here is one sentence to introduce diffusion: a diffusion model is a network that can denoise at every noise level, plus a sampler that starts from pure Gaussian noise and denoises repeatedly.
Step 1 · the forward process (fixed, not learned)

Destroy images with noise: $x_t=\alpha_t x_0+\sigma_t\epsilon$

Any noise level $t$ can be sampled in one shot, so training never has to simulate a chain.

We start with the forward process: add Gaussian noise to a clean image, a little more at each step, until only noise is left. The time t marks how far along we are, so read it as the noise level. This process is fixed. Nothing here is learned. Because the noise is Gaussian, you can jump to any noise level directly. In the title's equation, the noisy image is alpha times the clean image plus sigma times the noise, and the curves of alpha and sigma are the noise schedule. In this figure, we show the variance-preserving cosine schedule, where alpha squared plus sigma squared always equals one.
Step 2 · training

Training is plain regression: predict the noise

DDPM objective$$\mathcal L=\mathbb E_{x_0,t,\epsilon}\,\big\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\big\|^2$$
  • No discriminator, no adversarial game
  • A denoising autoencoder trained at all noise levels at once

One MSE loss means it scales like supervised learning: bigger model + more data = better samples.

Training is just as simple: mix a random image with Gaussian noise at a random noise level, and ask the network, which we call the denoiser, to recover the added noise. The loss is the squared error on that noise: plain regression. That is the whole objective of DDPM, denoising diffusion probabilistic models, the 2020 paper that made diffusion work. Compare a GAN, where a generator is trained against a discriminator: that game is unstable and can collapse onto a few kinds of images. Here there is no game, so diffusion scales like supervised learning.
Step 3 · sampling

Generation = start from pure noise, denoise step by step

1000
network calls per sample (DDPM)
noise → layout
early steps: global structure, colour
→ detail
late steps: texture, edges

Like sculpting: start from a block of noise and chip away what does not look like an image.

To generate, we run it backwards: start from pure Gaussian noise and call the denoiser again and again, removing a little noise each time. Each row is one image being generated, from left to right, and each picture is the network's current guess of the final clean image. Notice the order: the early steps fix the layout and the colours, and the late steps only add texture. Each step is one network call, and DDPM needed about a thousand of them per image. It took researchers six years to bring that down to one step. Most models run this in the latent space of an autoencoder, where the image is compressed, rather than on pixels.
Why it works · the score

A denoiser secretly knows which way is data

Denoising = score estimation$$\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\approx-\sigma_t\,\nabla_x\log p_t(x_t)$$

Arrows: the exact score of a toy 2-D mixture. Dots: Langevin dynamics, i.e. follow the arrows plus a little noise, while the noise level anneals from 1 → 0.

Predicting the noise = knowing, at every noise level, the direction toward more likely data.

Why does predicting noise work? The best noise prediction equals minus sigma times the gradient of the log density of the noisy data, a result known as Tweedie's formula. That gradient is called the score: it points toward more likely images. So a denoiser also gives you the score, and training it this way is called denoising score matching. In the visualization, the data is a two-moons mixture of Gaussians, so the score is computed exactly. The dots start as noise. At high noise, the arrows are smooth and pull everything toward the data. As the noise shrinks, the dots settle onto the moons. That is annealed Langevin dynamics: follow the arrows plus a little noise while the noise shrinks. It is the sampler of NCSN, the noise-conditional score network, which we will introduce later.
Three languages, one model

Papers switch between three views

2015 · DDPM 2020

Variational

$p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)$

learn each reverse step; walk the Markov chain back

NCSN 2019 · Score SDE 2020

Score

$\nabla_x\log p_t(x)$

learn the uphill direction; Langevin / reverse SDE

DDIM · PF-ODE · FM / RF 2022

ODE / flow

$\tfrac{dx}{dt}=v_\theta(x,t)$

learn a velocity field; integrate an ODE

Same trained network, three readings, so results transfer freely between the three literatures.

Papers describe this one model in three different languages. [click] Variational: a hierarchical model whose reverse steps, each from one noise level to a slightly cleaner one, are learned. Score: learn the score, and sample with Langevin dynamics or a reverse-time SDE, a stochastic differential equation that adds a little noise at every instant. ODE, or flow: learn a velocity that moves noise toward data, and integrate that ordinary differential equation numerically. They are actually talking about the same thing, and they can be unified, as we will see later.
One network, two samplers

SDE and ODE samplers reach the same distribution

The ODE has no randomness: sampling becomes numerical integration, and noise ↔ image is invertible.

There are two ways to run the reverse process. On the left, the SDE sampler adds fresh noise at every step, so the paths jitter. On the right, the deterministic sampler, the probability-flow ODE, adds no noise after the start, so the paths are smooth. Yet at every moment, both clouds of points have the same distribution. This deterministic view brings two things. Sampling becomes numerical integration, so better solvers make it faster. And you can run it backwards, from a real image to its noise, which editing relies on.
Parameterizations

ε, x₀ or v: same model, different weighting

ε → x₀ (given xₜ)$\hat x_0=(x_t-\sigma_t\hat\epsilon)/\alpha_t$
v-prediction · tangent of the arc$v=\alpha_t\,\epsilon-\sigma_t\,x_0$
flow matching · along the chord$x_t=(1-t)\,x_0+t\,\epsilon,\;\; \tfrac{dx_t}{dt}=\epsilon-x_0$

Knowing $x_t$, each target is a linear function of the others; they differ in error amplification per noise level.

So far, the network predicts the noise. It could also predict the clean image, or a mix of the two called the velocity. Given the noisy input, each one can be computed from the others. The difference is which noise levels the loss cares about most, and how much a small error grows when you convert one target into another. Geometrically, with the variance-preserving schedule, the noisy image sits on a quarter circle between the image and the noise, and the velocity points along the arc. Two newer methods, flow matching and rectified flow, use a straight line instead, and predict its direction: the noise minus the clean image.
Guidance · the setting every system uses

Classifier-free guidance: overshoot the condition

CFG at every step$$\begin{aligned}\tilde\epsilon&=\epsilon_\theta(x_t,\varnothing)\\&+w\big[\epsilon_\theta(x_t,c)-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,\varnothing)\big]\end{aligned}$$

Train with the condition randomly dropped, so one network gives both terms. Click w: 0 = unconditional, 1 = plain conditional, > 1 = guided.

One setting trades diversity for fidelity to the prompt; almost every text-to-image or video system uses it.

Here the model is conditioned: it is also told which class we want, just as a text-to-image model is given a prompt. Conditioning alone samples the class faithfully, but the results often look bland. Classifier-free guidance, or CFG, fixes this. In training, the condition is sometimes dropped, so one network learns to predict both with and without it. At sampling time, we push from the unconditional prediction toward the conditional one, and past it, by a factor called the guidance scale. In the toy, the target class is the coloured blobs. At scale zero, the model samples both classes. At scale one, only the target class. And a larger scale pushes the samples into the most typical part of the class: sharper, but less diverse. The cost is two network calls per step, but this one setting trades diversity for fidelity, and almost every image and video system uses it.
Conditioning

Three ways a condition gets in

Modulate · AdaGN / adaLN

global vectors: timestep, class, pooled text

Cross-attention

token sequences: text from CLIP / T5

Concat / joint attention

spatial images, or text + image jointly

Global signals modulate normalization; sequences enter by attention; spatial signals are concatenated.

How does a condition get in? Global signals, like the noise level or a class label, go through a small network that sets the scale and shift of the normalization layers. Token sequences, like a text prompt, enter by cross-attention: image features are the queries, and text tokens the keys and values. Spatial conditions, like a low-resolution image to upscale, are concatenated with the noisy input. And newer Transformers such as MMDiT run joint attention over text and image tokens.
Why diffusion displaced GANs after 2021

Stable, complete, editable, but slow

MSE
stable training

no generator–discriminator balance, so scaling is safe

ELBO
covers the distribution

likelihood-based: dropping modes is penalized

∀ t
editable

guide, constrain, invert, inpaint at any step

×1000
the price

many network calls per sample → chapter 6

The first three made it win; the fourth set the research agenda for six years.

Why did diffusion displace GANs? [click] First, training is one regression loss, so it scales without balancing a generator against a discriminator. Second, the objective, a bound on the likelihood called the ELBO, punishes the model for missing any part of the data, so samples stay diverse. Third, because generation is iterative, you can intervene at every step. [click] The cost is speed: tens to a thousand network calls per sample. We will show how to reduce that to one network evaluation.

Read every milestone in this talk as a move along one of these rows.

Our talk will cover the following topics step by step. The training target moved from the noise to the velocity, and recently back to the clean image. The number of steps went from a thousand to one. The backbone went from the U-Net, a convolutional network that downsamples and then upsamples, to Transformers. Where we denoise moved from pixels to autoencoder latents and video latents, and lately to latents from recognition models, or back to pixels. The condition went from class labels to text encoders and language models, until diffusion became the image part of a multimodal language model. And the training signal went from web captions to captions written by models, and then to reinforcement learning. The last item in each row is roughly where we are today.

Chapter 1 · Origins & revival · 2015 → 2020

From a 2015 idea
to one SDE

2015 origin why five quiet years? NCSN DDPM DDIM Score SDE
Now back to the beginning: how a 2015 idea grew into one framework by 2020.
Diffusion probabilistic models · Sohl-Dickstein et al. · 2015.03

2015: learn to undo the noise

forward step · fixed$$q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})=\mathcal N\big(\sqrt{1-\beta_t}\,x_{t-1},\;\beta_t I\big)$$

shrink a little, add a little noise, repeat

Tiny steps ⇒ the reverse step is ≈ Gaussian too (Feller, 1949) ⇒ fit it with an ELBO

Destroy data slowly with a fixed process, then learn to undo each tiny step: the whole idea, in 2015.

In 2015, the pioneering work proposed the whole idea of "add noise step by step, learn to remove it step by step". The top row adds a little Gaussian noise to a toy spiral at every step, until only noise is left. The reverse chain, in the bottom row, is learned. The key is a classic result: if each step is small enough, the reverse step is also close to a Gaussian. So a complicated distribution becomes many simple Gaussian steps, and the network predicts each step's mean, the average slightly cleaner image.
2015 → 2020

A 2015 idea, then five quiet years. Why?

vs

2015: add noise step by step, learn to undo it

speaker interpretation
  • Quality: far behind GANs
  • No recipe yet: ε-prediction, simple loss, attention U-Net
  • Speed: hundreds to thousands of steps vs one GAN pass

One reading: the 2015 idea was right but lacked a training recipe; DDPM supplied one. Speed came later.

So why did the paper go quiet for about five years? My interpretation is: First, the sample quality was not as good as that of GANs and VAEs. Second, the key recipe was missing: the model was not trained very well. Third, sampling took hundreds or thousands of network calls, where a GAN needs one. And you can see the quality gap here: the 2015 samples on the left are blurry, while DDPM's samples on the right show recognisable objects.
NCSN · Song & Ermon · 2019.07

NCSN: add noise on purpose, at many scales

Big noise fills empty space so the score is learnable everywhere; then shrink the noise, coarse to fine.

In 2019, Song and Ermon at Stanford proposed the score route. They think that plain score matching fails on images for three reasons: data lies near a low-dimensional manifold, the score is badly estimated in low-density regions — on the left, it is accurate only inside the boxes — and Langevin dynamics mixes slowly between modes. Their fix is to perturb the data with many noise levels, from large to small, and train one network, conditioned on the noise level, with denoising score matching.
DDPM · Ho, Jain & Abbeel · 2020.06

DDPM: the 2015 chain + one regression loss

the key simplification $$-\mathrm{ELBO}\simeq\sum_t w_t\,\mathbb E\big\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\big\|^2\;\xrightarrow{\;w_t\,\to\,1\;}\;L_{\text{simple}}$$

each term = denoising at one noise level; set all weights to 1

recipe reused for years
T = 1000linear β: 10⁻⁴ → 0.02 U-Net + attention at 16² fixed variancesinusoidal t

DDPM showed the 2015 objective is weighted noise regression, dropped the weights, and added a modern U-Net.

DDPM keeps the chain but changes three things. One: any noise level can be sampled in one shot, because the forward process has a closed form. Two: what the network predicts. The 2015 network predicted the mean of each Gaussian reverse step, the average slightly cleaner image. DDPM predicts the added noise instead. The mean follows from it, so nothing is lost. Then the objective splits into one weighted denoising term per noise level, and every term asks the same thing: predict the noise. DDPM simply drops the weights, and that plain loss became the starting point for the models that followed. Three: careful engineering. This paper explored how to choose the number of steps and the noise schedule, and set up the base design: a U-Net with self-attention and a time embedding.
DDPM · results

It finally works: GAN-level images, no GAN

3.17
FID · CIFAR-10 (lower is better)
9.46
Inception score · CIFAR-10

LSUN 256²: comparable to ProgressiveGAN, with no discriminator

First diffusion samples that could stand next to GANs, from a network trained with one MSE loss.

The results restarted the field. Here are its churches, bedrooms and cats, about as good as a strong GAN of the time. And it got there with no adversarial training, just one regression loss. The recipe on the previous slide became the base for diffusion models. But two problems remained in 2020: GANs still won on ImageNet, and sampling was slow.
DDPM · what the noise levels mean

Noise level = level of abstraction

Noisy early steps decide coarse attributes, late steps decide fine detail: diffusion generates coarse to fine.

What does each noise level decide? In the top rows, each group of faces starts from the same partly noisy image, and only the remaining steps use fresh noise. Sharing only the pure noise gives unrelated faces. Sharing a middle step keeps coarse attributes like sunglasses, and sharing a late step keeps almost everything. Below, two real faces are noised, mixed and denoised, and the in-between images stay realistic faces. So the early steps decide the coarse content, and the late steps the fine detail.
DDIM · Song, Meng & Ermon · 2020.10

DDIM: same network, no randomness, far fewer steps

one DDIM step (η = 0)$$x_{t-1}=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\;\hat x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\;\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)$$

① predict clean $\hat x_0$ ② re-noise it with the same $\epsilon$

10–50×
faster, no retraining
50
DDIM steps: original SD script

Keep the trained DDPM, change only the sampler: deterministic steps let you skip most of the chain.

Next came DDIM, denoising diffusion implicit models. The DDPM loss only depends on how a clean image is noised to each level, not on how the steps chain together. So a trained DDPM network can be reused with other sampling processes, even ones with no randomness. In the figure, the deterministic top rows stay sharp even with few steps. In DDIM, each step predicts the clean image, then re-noises it to the lower level along the same noise direction. The result is a large wall-clock speed-up, and we can generally use DDIM with 50 steps.
DDIM · a deterministic map noise ↔ image

Fixed noise → fixed image: invert and edit

DDIM inversion
Prompt-to-Prompt 2022.08Null-text Inversion 2022.11
approximate: error grows with large CFG

With no randomness, noise and image map one-to-one, so a real photo can be encoded, then re-generated.

With no randomness, the starting noise fully determines the image. In the top left, each column starts from the same noise and uses very different step counts, yet gives nearly the same face, which the paper calls consistency. Below it, blending two starting noises moves smoothly from one bedroom to another. On the right, the process runs backwards, encoding a real image into its noise. Regenerate with a new condition, and you get an edit. This DDIM inversion became the basic operation for real-image and video editing.
Score SDE · Song et al. · Stanford / Google Brain · 2020.11

Score SDE: one equation for NCSN and DDPM

probability-flow ODE · white lines
$\displaystyle\frac{dx}{dt}=f(x,t)-\tfrac12\,g(t)^2\,\nabla_x\log p_t(x)$

same marginals as the SDE, no noise: exact likelihood, invertible

NCSN (2019: one net, many noise levels) = variance-exploding (VE)
DDPM = variance-preserving (VP)

Pick a noising SDE; running it backwards needs only the score, which a denoiser already learns.

Score SDE moved diffusion to continuous time. The forward process becomes a stochastic differential equation, at the top left, where the image drifts and gets a little noise at every instant. NCSN and DDPM are special cases of it. Its time reversal is also an SDE, and the only unknown is the score at each time, which denoising score matching learns. Each SDE also has a noise-free twin with the same distributions, the probability-flow ODE, drawn as white lines. It allows faster solvers, exact likelihoods, and encoding an image into noise and back. The SDE noise washes out accumulated errors, while the ODE is invertible and allows big steps.
Score SDE · results · 2020.11

CIFAR records, 1024² faces, no-retrain editing

CIFAR-10 FID ↓ · unconditional · lower is better

One score model, many tasks: conditions are added at sampling time, so inpainting needs no retraining.

Here are its results. On CIFAR-10, a standard benchmark of small images, it set a new record for sample quality, ahead of both NCSN and DDPM. They also achieve the first high-fidelity, high-resolution generation by a score-based model. Conditions can also be added at sampling time, by steering each step toward the condition. So one model fills in missing regions and colorizes photos, on the right, with no retraining.
Chapter 1 · recap

Two routes, one framework

By the end of 2020: one framework, one recipe, CIFAR records. Not yet: beating GANs on ImageNet, or speed.

Let me put all of this into one picture. Two routes started separately: the score route on top, leading to NCSN in 2019, and the variational route below, from the 2015 paper to DDPM. What joins them is the identity we saw early on: a denoiser is a score estimator. [click] Score SDE merged both routes, and DDIM turned out to be a step-by-step version of the same probability-flow ODE. [click] Almost everything later grows from here: guidance, flow matching, faster sampling, and editing by inversion. What was still missing in 2020 was speed, and a win over GANs on ImageNet.

Chapter 2 · Beating GANs · 2021 → 2022

Beating GANs, and the
guidance scale

iDDPM ADM classifier guidance CFG EDM
Next: how diffusion overtook GANs, the generator-versus-discriminator models that led image generation at the time. Between 2021 and 2022, diffusion passed them, and along the way it gained the guidance that nearly every model uses today.
The gap · iDDPM 2021.02 vs BigGAN

Diffusion wins at 64², but GANs still own 256²

ImageNet FID ↓
Diffusion lacked

① a systematically ablated U-Net

② a diversity ↔ fidelity control

Diffusion led on small images; GANs led at 256² and had a fidelity control.

Let's start with where things stood in early 2021. An OpenAI team had just published Improved DDPM, a carefully tuned version of the original recipe. On small, 64 by 64 ImageNet images, its largest model already beat BigGAN-deep, the strongest GAN. But at the standard 256 by 256, even a two-stage cascade, a small model plus an upsampler, was still far from BigGAN-deep. Their next paper introduced ADM, short for ablated diffusion model, and named two reasons for the gap. First, GAN architectures had been tuned for years, while diffusion still used the original U-Net. Second, GANs have the truncation trick: sample the input noise closer to the centre of the Gaussian, and samples become more typical and sharper, but less diverse. Diffusion had no way to make that trade.
ADM · Dhariwal & Nichol · OpenAI · 2021.05

Fix 1: a U-Net tuned by systematic ablation

Early 2021: GANs still led ImageNet at 256².

No single trick: more attention, BigGAN-style blocks, and timestep + class steering every block.

ADM's first fix was the architecture. The team scored each change with FID, the Fréchet Inception Distance, a standard measure of how far generated images are from real ones, where lower is better. They ablated the U-Net on ImageNet 128, tracking FID against training wall-clock time. The final design adds more attention, BigGAN-style residual blocks, and adaptive group normalization, where the noise level and class label set a scale and shift inside every block. In the plot, the pink curve combines the helpful changes, and it stays below the blue baseline throughout training. This U-Net became the standard backbone until about 2023.
ADM · classifier guidance · 2021

Fix 2: a classifier steers every denoising step

guided score$$\nabla\log\tilde p(x_t|y)=\nabla\log p_\theta(x_t)+s\,\nabla\log p_\phi(y|x_t)$$

model’s direction + s × “look more like class y”

A classifier nudges every step toward the class; its volume s trades variety (recall) for fidelity (precision).

The second fix was classifier guidance. You train a separate classifier that recognises the class even in noisy images. At every denoising step, you take its gradient, which points toward looking more like the class, multiply it by a guidance scale, and add it to the diffusion model's score. Intuitively, this samples from the joint distribution of the sample and the condition. In practice, it is a first-order shift of each step's Gaussian mean. A larger scale raises precision, meaning realistic, on-class samples, and lowers recall, meaning coverage of the real variety. In the left figure, at scale 1 the samples are barely corgis, at scale 10 clearly corgis, and more alike. On the right, at the same precision, guidance usually keeps more recall than the GAN truncation trick.
ADM-G · ImageNet 256² · 2021

Diffusion beats BigGAN, and covers more modes

4.59
FID ↓ · BigGAN-deep 6.95
0.52
recall ↑ · BigGAN-deep 0.28
precision: BigGAN-deep still higher, 0.87 vs 0.82

no guidance 10.94 · + upsampler 3.94 · 25 steps 5.44

First diffusion model to beat the best GAN on ImageNet 256², with far more varied samples.

Together, the two fixes let diffusion beat BigGAN on ImageNet at 256 by 256, with a better FID and much higher recall. Look at the flamingos: BigGAN's flocks all look alike, while ADM's mix close-ups, single birds and flocks. There was a price. ADM took far more training compute than BigGAN, and each image needs many network calls instead of one. But no GAN could match its mix of quality and variety.
CFG · Ho & Salimans · 2021.12

Drop the classifier: one network guides itself

Classifier guidance: ① extra noise-aware classifier
② no open-text labels · ③ adversarial-like gradients

Bayes · implicit classifier$$\nabla\log p(c|x)=\nabla\log p(x|c)-\nabla\log p(x)$$

conditional − unconditional pass = its gradient

Recap: ε(x,∅) + w·(ε(x,c) − ε(x,∅)), c dropped 10–20%

∅ → negative prompt→ GLIDE, DALL·E 2, Imagen, SD, DiT, video
no guidanceCFG · same seeds Ho & Salimans, 2021 · arXiv Fig. 7(a) vs 7(c), left halves (adapted)

One network, two passes: their gap is the guidance, no classifier needed.

Classifier guidance had three problems: a classifier that works at every noise level must be trained, for open text such a classifier is hard to define, and following a classifier's gradient resembles an adversarial attack. [click] Classifier-free guidance, or CFG, proposes to use one network to learn both the conditional and the unconditional model, by replacing the condition with a null token some of the time. As the equation shows, by Bayes' rule the difference between the two predictions is exactly the gradient of an implicit classifier, so no separate classifier is needed. On the right, unguided samples look blurry. With strong guidance, the same seeds give clear, recognisable objects. [click] CFG became a standard module of diffusion models.
CFG · the trade-off · 2021

Turn up w: sharper classes, less variety

1.55
best FID · ImageNet 64² · at w = 1.1

Inception Score keeps rising · FID falls, then rises

large w: saturated colours, lost diversity

More guidance makes samples more typical and polished, and also more alike.

In the figure, the guidance increases from left to right. The dogs get cleaner and more typical, but also more alike. The Inception Score, which rewards recognisable objects, keeps rising, while FID first improves, then gets worse as variety is lost. Too much guidance also over-saturates colours. Why push past the conditional model at all, when it already knows the class? Intuitively, guidance sharpens the implicit classifier, favouring images the model finds clearly recognisable as that class.
CFG · descendants · 2022 → 2025

CFG became the default, and a research field

Two passes per step became the norm; follow-ups make it cheaper, or keep the variety.

Classifier-free guidance became the default, and a research topic of its own. Users got negative prompts: put what you don't want where the empty condition was, and guidance pushes away from it. Two passes per step double the cost, which motivated guidance distillation, teaching one network to give the guided result in a single pass. Another study found that guidance hurts at high noise and barely matters at low noise, so it works best only in between. In the toy example, plain guidance leaves whole branches of the orange shape empty, while autoguidance, which guides with a weaker copy of the same model, keeps the variety. Even LLMs can use CFG.
EDM · Karras et al. · NVIDIA · 2022.06

EDM: one noise level σ, independent choices

all models: data + noise of level σ$$x=y+n,\;\; n\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2 I)$$$$\nabla_x\log p=\frac{D(x;\sigma)-x}{\sigma^2}$$

only σ and a denoiser D matter

σ = primer’s $\sigma_t/\alpha_t$ (noise-to-signal)

EDM writes every diffusion model in one notation, so each design choice can be swapped on its own.

By 2022, DDPM, DDIM and score SDEs each used their own notation. NVIDIA's EDM, short for elucidating the design space of diffusion models, rewrote them all in one form: a noisy image is a clean image plus Gaussian noise of level sigma. This sigma is the noise-to-signal ratio. In the table, each row is one design choice, such as the sampler, the noise levels used in training, or the loss weighting. Pink marks EDM's choice in each row. So is EDM a new model? Not really: it is a common language plus a tuned recipe, where each choice can be improved on its own.
EDM · sampler · 2022

Same weights, better sampler: better images, fewer steps

A better sampler alone improves an already-trained model: training and sampling are separate choices.

EDM also showed that the sampler is a design choice separate from training: keep the same trained network, change only the sampler, and you get better images in fewer steps, with no retraining.
Background: DALL·E 2 sample · Ramesh et al., 2022 · Fig. 1 (adapted)
03
Chapter 3 · 2021 → 2023

Text-to-image goes mainstream:
type a sentence,
get a picture

GLIDE DALL·E 2 Imagen Latent Diffusion Stable Diffusion DALL·E 3
Now we introduce how diffusion became the engine of open-domain text-to-image. Here, a picture emerges from noise, step by step, from a single sentence.
Context · 2021.12 → 2022.08

Eight months: from a GLIDE paper to open SD weights

8 months

In eight months, text-to-image went from an OpenAI paper to weights anyone could download.

This timeline shows how fast it all happened. In December 2021, GLIDE and the Latent Diffusion paper came out on the same day. DALL·E 2 was announced in April 2022, Google's Imagen followed in May, Midjourney opened a beta in July, and in August Stable Diffusion was released with open weights, which anyone could download and run. By late 2023, SDXL, a larger Stable Diffusion, along with Emu and DALL·E 3, shared most of the same ingredients.
GLIDE · Nichol et al. · OpenAI · 2021.12

GLIDE: text-conditioned diffusion beats DALL·E

87%
humans prefer GLIDE · photorealism
69%
humans prefer GLIDE · caption match

vs DALL·E with CLIP reranking
3.5B vs 12B parameters

A diffusion model fed the caption directly already beat the 12B autoregressive DALL·E in human ratings.

GLIDE took the ADM model and conditioned it on text: a text Transformer turns the caption into tokens that the U-Net's attention layers read. Human raters clearly preferred it to OpenAI's earlier DALL·E, both for photorealism and for matching the caption. And it used roughly the same training compute as DALL·E, with a much smaller model.
GLIDE · “a stained glass window of a panda eating bamboo”

CLIP guidance wins on CLIP score; humans pick CFG

CLIP guidance scores higher on CLIP, yet humans prefer CFG; the authors suspect it fools the scorer.

GLIDE also compared two kinds of guidance: following CLIP, a model that scores how well an image matches a caption, and classifier-free guidance. Surprisingly, CLIP guidance gets the higher CLIP score, yet humans prefer classifier-free guidance. The authors suspect that CLIP-guided images act like adversarial examples, fooling CLIP rather than looking better. From then on, DALL·E 2, Imagen and Stable Diffusion all used classifier-free guidance.
DALL·E 2 / unCLIP · Ramesh et al. · OpenAI · 2022.04

DALL·E 2: predict a CLIP image embedding, then decode

two stages$$P(x\mid y)=P(x\mid z_i,y)\,P(z_i\mid y)$$

exact, because the CLIP embedding $z_i$ is a fixed function of the image $x$

Split the job: first guess what CLIP would “see” in the picture, then paint pixels that match it.

DALL·E 2 took another route. Above the dotted line is CLIP, kept frozen: a text encoder and an image encoder, trained so that a caption and its matching picture get similar embeddings. Below it, generation happens in two stages. First, a prior turns the caption into the CLIP image embedding that a matching picture would have. Then a GLIDE-style diffusion decoder turns that embedding into an image, and upsamplers raise the resolution.
DALL·E 2 · what one embedding keeps and loses

The embedding keeps the gist, loses who is where

A CLIP vector captures what is in a picture, but only loosely which object has which color or where.

Going through one CLIP embedding has an upside. Encode any image, decode it again with new random seeds, and the variations keep its content and style while every detail changes. The downside is attribute binding, attaching each property to the right object. For "a red cube on top of a blue cube", DALL·E 2 often swaps colours or positions, while GLIDE gets it right more often. One CLIP vector captures what is in a picture, but only loosely which object is where. Text inside images was also poor.
Imagen · Saharia et al. · Google · 2022.05

Imagen: a bigger text encoder beats a bigger U-Net

4.6B
frozen T5-XXL text encoder

A pixel cascade: 64² → 256² → 1024²

Understanding the prompt was the bottleneck: a bigger frozen language model beat a bigger image model.

Google's Imagen asked where extra parameters help most. Growing the text encoder, which turns the prompt into embeddings, improves both image quality and how well images match the prompt. Growing the U-Net helps much less. So Imagen uses T5, a large text-only language model, kept frozen, so the text embeddings can be computed in advance. On simple captions, T5 and CLIP's text encoder are about equal, but on harder prompts, human raters preferred T5 in every category.
Imagen · the pixel cascade

Imagen is a three-stage pixel cascade on frozen T5

dynamic thresholding$$\hat x_0 \leftarrow \operatorname{clip}(\hat x_0,-s,s)\,/\,s$$

$s$ = a high percentile of $|\hat x_0|$, applied only if $s>1$: strong guidance without over-saturated colors

7.27
zero-shot COCO FID
11
DrawBench categories

Generate a tiny image, then upsample twice; every stage reads the same frozen text embedding.

Under the hood, Imagen works as a pixel cascade: a base model draws a tiny image, and two super-resolution models upscale it, all reading the same frozen T5 embedding. During training, each upscaler's low-resolution input is noised by a random amount, so errors from the stage before don't pile up. And dynamic thresholding allows strong guidance without over-saturated colours, by clipping and rescaling out-of-range values at every step.
Latent Diffusion · Rombach et al. · CompVis / Runway · 2021.12

Latent Diffusion: denoise a small latent, not pixels

LDM objective$$\mathcal L=\mathbb E\,\big\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta\big(z_t,t,\tau_\theta(y)\big)\big\|^2$$

the primer’s noise-prediction loss, applied to $z=\mathcal E(x)$ instead of pixels

An autoencoder handles pixel detail, so diffusion only models a compact latent and gets far cheaper.

Now the other route, Latent Diffusion. First, the autoencoder alone, in red. It is trained once, with perceptual and patch-adversarial losses plus a light KL or vector-quantization penalty, to map an image to a latent and back. [click] Then the whole diffusion process runs inside that small latent, shown in green. [click] Finally, conditioning. An encoder turns the text, or a layout, or a semantic map, into tokens that the U-Net reads through cross-attention. The loss is the usual noise-prediction loss, applied to the latent. On the right are samples from the paper's own text-to-image model.
Latent Diffusion · why a latent works

Compress away invisible bits, diffuse the semantics

Mild compression removes detail nobody sees; too little is slow, too much costs quality.

Why does a latent work? The curve on the left shows that most of the bits describing an image go to detail nobody can see. A pixel-space model learns to ignore that detail, but still pays for every pixel at every training and sampling step. So the autoencoder removes the invisible detail, and diffusion models the meaning. The plot on the right varies how much the autoencoder shrinks the image: no shrinking trains slowly, too much loses quality, and mild compression works best.
Stable Diffusion v1 · open weights · 2022.08

Stable Diffusion: open weights on a consumer GPU

860M
latent U-Net, f = 8
123M
frozen CLIP text

LAION-5B subsets · 512² · ~150k A100 GPU-hours

DiffusersAUTOMATIC1111ComfyUI
DreamBoothLoRAControlNet

Same latent recipe, but public weights: anyone could run it, fine-tune it and build tools on top.

Stable Diffusion v1 applies this latent recipe with a U-Net of under a billion parameters and a frozen CLIP text encoder. It was trained on subsets of LAION, a public web collection of image and caption pairs, with some captions dropped so that classifier-free guidance works. Its U-Net is essentially the same as the one in the Latent Diffusion paper, so the gains came from more data, a better text encoder and more training. And its public weights run on a single consumer graphics card.
DALL·E 3 · OpenAI · 2023.09 details undisclosed

DALL·E 3: the bottleneck was the captions

web alt-text

is he finished...just about!

short synthetic

a quilt with an iron on it.

descriptive synthetic · 95%

…patchwork design with pastel-colored strips of fabric and floral patterns…

Detailed training captions teach the model to follow long prompts.

DALL·E 3 found the remaining bottleneck in the captions. Web alt-text, the text attached to images online, is short, noisy and often unrelated: for this quilt, it is just "is he finished... just about!" So OpenAI trained a captioner that writes short or detailed descriptions, and recaptioned the whole training set. In the plot, descriptive captions beat short ones and raw alt-text, and keeping a few original captions stops the model from overfitting to the captioner's style. At generation time, GPT-4 expands short user prompts into detailed ones. Recaptioning then became a standard setup.
Synthesis · the 2023 default

By 2023 the recipe had converged

built largely from these parts
SDXL · 2023.07Emu · 2023.09DALL·E 3 · 2023.09 partly disclosed

Next: control and personalization on top of open SD (chapter 4)

Also: GLIDE (CFG for text)
and DALL·E 3 (recaptioned data)

By late 2023 most new systems used the same parts: a latent, a big text encoder, CFG and rich captions.

By 2023, the pieces had converged into one recipe. Latent Diffusion's autoencoder, usually called the VAE, provides the latent space. A big text encoder like T5, often with CLIP, reads the prompt. A U-Net reads the text through cross-attention, with classifier-free guidance. Training uses detailed synthetic captions, then a final fine-tune on hand-picked images, which Meta's Emu showed makes images more visually appealing. Two routes faded: the CLIP-embedding prior and pixel-space cascades. Classifier-free guidance, frozen language models and better captions all attacked one problem: making the model actually follow the prompt.

04
Chapter 4 · 2021 → 2025

Control, personalize, edit:
more than a prompt can say

SDEdit / Prompt-to-Prompt Textual Inversion DreamBooth LoRA ControlNet InstructPix2Pix FLUX.1 Kontext
Text-to-image now works, but a prompt cannot draw my own dog, hold a specific pose, or change only the sky. Next: three kinds of control beyond the prompt, namely personalization, spatial control and editing.
Context · 2021 → 2025

Text can’t say “my dog”, “this pose”, or “only here”

Personalize a subject, fix the layout, edit one detail: each got its own fix, then one model did all three.

The timeline has four lanes: personalization, spatial control, editing, and a newer route that feeds reference images straight into the model.
DreamBooth · Ruiz et al. · Google Research / BU · 2022.08

Teach the model one specific dog from 3–5 photos

prompt “a [V] dog” · prior-preservation loss $$\underbrace{\|\hat x_\theta(x_t,c_{[V]})-x\|^2}_{\text{learn this dog}}+\lambda\underbrace{\|\hat x_\theta(x^{pr}_{t'},c_{pr})-x^{pr}\|^2}_{\text{replay the model's own “a dog” samples}}$$

full fine-tune · ~1000 steps · ~5 min on one A100 (SD)

Bind a rare word to your subject, fine-tune the model, and replay its own samples so “dog” keeps its meaning.

Personalization first. Textual Inversion keeps the model frozen and learns the embedding of one new word to stand for your subject. But one vector can't hold much detail: in the bottom row on the right, the vase loses its shape. DreamBooth instead ties the subject to a rare word, as in "a V dog", and fine-tunes all of the model's weights on three to five photos. With so few photos, "dog" starts to mean only my dog. To prevent that, the original model first draws its own dog pictures, and training must keep reproducing them. The whole fine-tune takes only minutes on one GPU.
LoRA · Hu et al. · Microsoft · 2021.06 · on SD 2022.12

LoRA: ship a few-MB patch, not a GB checkpoint

frozen $W_0$ + low-rank patch$$W=W_0+\tfrac{\alpha}{r}\,BA$$

$B=0$: starts as the original model

1–6 MB
per file · ~2× faster than full DreamBooth (cloneofsimo README)

Freeze the big weights, learn a tiny low-rank add-on; share it, stack it, dial its strength.

Fine-tuning normally means a full new copy of the model. LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, freezes each weight matrix and learns a small correction, the product of two thin matrices, B and A. B starts at zero, so training starts exactly at the original model. We will see this trick twice more. In the video, scaling the correction from zero to one blends the original model into the fine-tuned one. Gigabyte checkpoints became shareable files of a few megabytes.
ControlNet · Zhang, Rao & Agrawala · Stanford · 2023.02

ControlNet: a trainable copy that starts silent

one ControlNet block $$y_c=\mathcal F(x;\Theta)+\mathcal Z\big(\mathcal F(x+\mathcal Z(c;\Theta_{z1});\Theta_c);\Theta_{z2}\big)$$

locked block + zero conv(copy(input + zero conv(condition)))

Canny edgesoutput Zhang et al., 2023 · Fig. 1 (adapted)

“masterpiece of fairy tale, giant deer, golden antlers”

Freeze Stable Diffusion; a copy reads the sketch or pose and joins through layers that start at zero.

Next, spatial control. A prompt cannot pin down a pose or a layout. [click] ControlNet freezes Stable Diffusion and trains a copy of its encoder, the downsampling half of the U-Net. On the right is the condition alone, an edge map of a deer. A few small convolutions feed it into the copy. [click] The copy's outputs are added back through zero convolutions, layers whose weights start at zero, the same trick as in LoRA. Now the output appears, a deer that follows those edges. At the start of training the network is exactly Stable Diffusion, yet the zero convolutions still learn, so the copy's influence grows gradually from zero instead of disrupting the model.
ControlNet · one recipe, many conditions

Any spatial map works: edges, depth, pose, segments

scribbleZhang et al., 2023
normal mapZhang et al., 2023
depthZhang et al., 2023
soft edgesZhang et al., 2023
segmentationZhang et al., 2023
poseZhang et al., 2023

left of slider: condition · right: SD output, empty prompt · crops of Fig. 7

Same frozen SD, one trainable encoder copy per condition: edges, depth, pose, segments, scribbles.

Each pair first shows the condition, then the output, all generated with an empty prompt. With the sliders partway, you see condition and result side by side. Each condition type gets its own ControlNet, and several can be stacked. On the right, during training, the output ignores the edges for a long time, then, all at once, it follows them. Later, base models such as Qwen-Image-Edit learned to read these maps directly, with no separate ControlNet.
SDEdit 2021 · Prompt-to-Prompt 2022

Editing without training: noise it, or steer attention

strokesSDEdit Meng et al., 2021 · Fig. 1 (adapted)

SDEdit: noise to $t_0$, then denoise; img2img “strength” = $t_0$.

“…bicycle”“…car” Hertz et al., 2022 · Fig. 1 (adapted)

Prompt-to-Prompt: swap one word, keep the cross-attention maps: same layout.

Catch: real photos need inversion first; Null-text Inversion takes minutes each.

Early editing hacked the sampler: partly re-noise a picture, or reuse which word was drawn where.

Now editing. The first methods were sampler tricks that need no training. Take this rough painting of a castle. SDEdit adds some noise, then denoises, and out comes a realistic castle in the same layout. That is the strength slider in image-to-image. Halfway, you see both. The row below shows the trade-off: a little noise stays faithful to the strokes, while a lot looks realistic but drifts away from them. On the right, Prompt-to-Prompt steers attention instead. The original is a cat on a bicycle. Each word has a cross-attention map, which says where that word is drawn. Keep the maps, swap bicycle for car, and the scene stays. Side by side, the layout holds. But a real photo must first be inverted, running the sampler backwards to find its noise, and doing that accurately takes minutes per photo.
InstructPix2Pix · Brooks, Holynski & Efros · Berkeley · 2022.11

No editing dataset? Generate one with GPT-3 + SD

700
human-written edits
↓
GPT-3 → SD + Prompt-to-Prompt
→ CLIP filter
454,445
synthetic training pairs

Teach GPT-3 to write edits, let Stable Diffusion paint before/after pairs, and get a huge synthetic dataset.

None of these tricks took a plain instruction like "make it snowy". InstructPix2Pix turned editing into supervised learning and manufactured the data. People wrote a few hundred examples, each a caption, an instruction and the edited caption. GPT-3 was fine-tuned on them and wrote many more. Then Stable Diffusion, with Prompt-to-Prompt, turned each pair of captions into a before-and-after pair of images. That idea, using big models to make training data, outlived the model itself.
InstructPix2Pix · no inversion, no per-image tuning

One instruction, one sampling run, two guidance scales

input“turn her into a snake lady” Brooks et al., 2022
Fig. 2(d) (adapted)
two-condition CFG $$\begin{aligned}\tilde\epsilon=\;&\epsilon_{\varnothing\varnothing}\\&+s_I\,(\epsilon_{I\varnothing}-\epsilon_{\varnothing\varnothing})\\&+s_T\,(\epsilon_{IT}-\epsilon_{I\varnothing})\end{aligned}$$

$s_I$: stay close to the image
$s_T$: follow the instruction

Trained only on synthetic pairs, it edits real photos from a plain sentence in seconds, no inversion.

The model starts from Stable Diffusion. The input image enters as extra input channels whose weights start at zero, so again training begins at the pretrained model. Dropping the image, the text or both in training gives two guidance scales: one to stay close to the image, one to follow the instruction. In the grid, the edit grows stronger to the right and stays closer to the statue going down. Here is the painting, and here is the edit, "turn her into a snake lady": one sampling run, no inversion, and although it was trained only on generated pairs, it works on real images.
FLUX.1 Kontext · Black Forest Labs · 2025.05

Kontext: the reference image is just more tokens

Training: the usual denoising loss, on the target tokens only; drop the context ($y=\varnothing$) and it is plain text-to-image.

No side network: append the reference image’s tokens to the sequence and let attention do the rest.

By 2024, open models had one add-on per control, mostly on U-Nets. Transformers see an image as a sequence of patches, called tokens, so a simpler route appeared: put the condition image's tokens into the same sequence. FLUX.1 Kontext scales this up, fine-tuning the FLUX.1 Transformer on millions of context, instruction and target triplets. [click] The context image goes through the frozen VAE, and its tokens are appended after the target tokens. [click] The position encoding, which tells the model where each token sits, gives the context image its own offset, so the model can tell the two images apart. Only the target tokens are noised. The price is a sequence about twice as long.
FLUX.1 Kontext · multi-turn consistency

Same character, new scene: edit after edit

One reference image plus a sentence keeps a character consistent; no per-character fine-tuning needed.

This also enables multi-round editing: each output becomes the context for the next instruction.
Chapter 4 · takeaways

Start from identity, then let data do the work

step 0 = pretrained model
LoRA$B=0\;\Rightarrow\;BA=0$
ControlNet$\mathcal Z(\cdot)=0$
InstructPix2Pix$W_{\text{new channels}}=0$

U-Net era: side branches
ControlNet · IP-Adapter

→

Transformer era: conditions are tokens
OmniGen · Kontext · Qwen-Image-Edit

+

LoRA never left
FLUX · Qwen · video

Every add-on starts as a no-op on the pretrained model; in Transformers, conditions become tokens.

Let me sum up with three lessons. First, start from the pretrained model. LoRA's zero matrix, ControlNet's zero convolutions and the zero input channels of InstructPix2Pix all make training begin exactly there. Second, data beats architecture, and big models can synthesize the paired data. Third, the backbone decides how conditions enter: side branches in U-Nets, plain tokens in Transformers. And LoRA never went away: it is still the usual way to customize today's image and video models.
Background: SD3 samples · Esser et al., 2024 · Fig. 1 (crop)
05
Chapter 5 · 2022 → 2026

The recipe converges:
DiT + flow matching

DiT flow matching / rectified flow SD3 · MMDiT FLUX.1 REPA RAE JiT
Next, the recipe itself changes. In 2022, the standard model was a U-Net that predicts noise inside a VAE latent, and reads the prompt through a CLIP or T5 text encoder. Then two of those parts changed. The backbone became a plain Transformer, called DiT, short for diffusion Transformer. And the objective became predicting velocity along straight lines between noise and data.
DiT · Peebles & Xie · 2022.12

A plain ViT on latent patches replaces the U-Net

Diffusion no longer needs a hand-built U-Net: a standard Transformer on latent patches does the job.

Before DiT, almost every denoiser was a convolutional U-Net, and nobody knew if the convolution's bias toward local structure was essential. DiT keeps the VAE, cuts the latent into small patches, one token each, and feeds them to a nearly standard Vision Transformer, as on the left. Only the denoiser drops convolutions, while the VAE stays convolutional. Why give up that bias? The VAE already handles local texture. And as in image recognition, with enough data and compute, a model that scales well beats hand-built assumptions.
DiT · scaling

Diffusion gets a scaling law: Gflops predict FID

2.27
FID · DiT-XL/2
CFG 1.5
3.60
previous best
diffusion · LDM

Deeper, wider or more tokens all lower FID: diffusion inherits the Transformer scaling playbook.

DiT measures model size by compute, in gigaflops, billions of operations, per forward pass. On the left, each point is a model. Going deeper, going wider, or using smaller patches and so more tokens all lower the FID, where lower is better. And compute predicts the FID better than the parameter count does. The largest model beat the best previous diffusion model on ImageNet. After DiT, progress came from bigger Transformers, more tokens and more data, not hand-tuned U-Nets.
Flow matching · 2022.09–10

Flow matching: regress velocity along a straight line

straight path · t = 0 data, t = 1 noise$x_t=(1-t)\,x_0+t\,\epsilon$
regress its velocity · simulation-free$\mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}\,\big\|v_\theta(x_t,t)-(\epsilon-x_0)\big\|^2$

It learns the expected velocity of the lines through (xₜ, t).

SD3 calls this rectified flow.

Rectified Flow Stochastic Interpolants Flow Matching

Training needs no ODE simulation: just regression at random points on noise–data lines.

Now the objective. In late 2022, three papers proposed nearly the same idea. It is the straight path we met at the start: pick a straight line between noise and data, and regress the velocity along it, which is simply the noise minus the image. Training is plain regression: you never have to run the model along a path while training. Only generation runs the ODE, from noise to image. Here is the lion at time zero, clean, and at time one, pure noise. Halfway, it is an even mix. The network sees only this mix and the time, not which pair made it, so it learns the average of all the velocities through this point. Once more, the whole path: a steady fade from image to noise. The three papers differ mainly in emphasis, and today the names flow matching and rectified flow are used almost interchangeably.
Flow matching · what the network learns

Straight training lines, but the learned flow curves

With Gaussian noise, FM is diffusion with $\alpha_t=1-t,\ \sigma_t=t$: the gain is parameterization and weighting.

Straight paths need few steps, but plain flow matching does not learn them; reflow (right) retrains to straighten.

So what does the network learn? On the left, for a toy dataset of eight clusters, the training targets are straight lines from random noise to random points, and many of them cross. In the middle is the learned flow. Where lines cross, the network predicts their average, so its paths bend, and two big straight steps, the colored dots, miss the clusters. On the right is the fix. Run the trained model to turn many noise samples into images, then train a new model on exactly those pairs. This is called reflow. Now each noise sample has its own image, the lines stop crossing, the paths come out nearly straight, and two steps land on the clusters. With thirty-two small steps instead, the curved paths reach the clusters too. So straightness is about cost: curved paths need many steps, straight ones only a few. With just two steps, only the straight paths land. InstaFlow applied this to Stable Diffusion: reflow, then distillation, where a fast student copies a slow model.
Flow matching vs diffusion

Gaussian FM is diffusion with a different schedule

the straight line is a schedule$\alpha_t=1-t,\;\;\sigma_t=t$
v is a reparameterization$\hat x_0=x_t-t\,\hat v$

DDIM = Euler on this schedule.

What matters: loss weighting and output parameterization.

Flow matching did not beat diffusion as a family; it found simpler, better-tuned defaults.

Is flow matching better than diffusion, then? With Gaussian noise, the two are mathematically equivalent. The straight line is just one noise schedule, velocity is just another way to write noise prediction, and on this schedule the deterministic DDIM sampler is exactly the simplest solver for the flow. On the left is diffusion, on the right flow matching, on the same toy, and neither set of paths is straight. What changes results is how the loss is weighted across noise levels, and what the network outputs. So flow matching brought better default settings, not a fundamentally better kind of model.
Stable Diffusion 3 · Esser et al. · Stability AI · 2024.03

SD3 tests 61 recipes: rectified flow + logit-normal wins

timestep sampling · train the middle most$\mathrm{logit}(t)\sim\mathcal{N}(m,s^2)$
resolution shift · 3.0 at 1024²$t_m=\dfrac{\alpha\,t_n}{1+(\alpha-1)\,t_n},\ \ \alpha=\sqrt{m/n}$

Train mid noise levels most and shift toward noise at high resolution; the shift lives on in FLUX and video.

So which defaults work best? Stable Diffusion 3, or SD3, tested this at scale in 2024. It compared dozens of combinations of objective and timestep sampling, meaning how often each noise level is trained. Rectified flow won, with the middle noise levels trained most. Why the middle? Near clean data the job is easy, near pure noise you can only guess an average, so content is decided in between. And at high resolution, neighbouring pixels are so alike that the same noise destroys less, so timesteps are shifted toward more noise. On the left, the top row, without the shift, looks oversaturated, and the bottom row, with it, looks clean. The idea came from an earlier paper, simple diffusion, and the shift is now a standard setting in today's image and video models.
SD3 · MMDiT

MMDiT: text and image tokens attend to each other

Text tokens now update from the image too; per-modality weights beat shared weights and cross-attention.

SD3 also changed the architecture, and as the samples on the right show, it can spell. With cross-attention, the image reads the text tokens, but the text is never updated. [click] MMDiT, short for multimodal DiT, keeps separate weights for text and image tokens, but in every layer they share one joint attention, where every token attends to every other, so information flows both ways. This improved prompt following and typography, and in SD3's tests it beat both cross-attention and shared weights.
FLUX.1 · Black Forest Labs · 2024.08

FLUX.1: SD3's recipe at 12B, the new open standard

[pro]

API only

[dev]

open weights · CFG baked in · non-commercial

[schnell]

1–4 steps · Apache 2.0

[dev] needs tens of steps; [schnell] is distilled → chapter 6.

Technically a refinement of SD3; arguably its impact was the ecosystem, replacing SDXL as the open-weight default.

FLUX.1, in 2024, scaled the SD3 recipe to twelve billion parameters, with MMDiT-style blocks first and then single-stream blocks with shared weights, shown on the right. Its downloadable dev version takes the guidance scale as an input, so guidance costs one network call instead of two. FLUX.1 soon replaced SDXL as the default open model.
REPA · Yu et al. · 2024.10

REPA: align with DINOv2, train >17.5× faster

>17.5×
faster SiT training

flow loss − patch-wise cosine to DINOv2$\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{flow}}-\lambda\,\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_n\cos\big(y^{[n]}_{\text{DINO}},\,h_\phi(h_t^{[n]})\big)$

One reading: much of diffusion training is representation learning, which frozen DINOv2 features can supply.

Next, training speed. Is training slow because the model must learn what things are from scratch? REPA, short for representation alignment, adds one extra loss. Patch by patch, it pulls the denoiser's early features toward the features that DINOv2, a frozen pretrained image encoder, extracts from the clean image. With this extra loss, a diffusion Transformer reaches the same quality many times faster. On the left, from the same noise, REPA's samples in the bottom row become recognizable much earlier than the baseline's. The lesson: much of diffusion training is really spent learning what things are, and a pretrained encoder can supply that. Its limitation is the external encoder, which a later method, Self-Flow, tries to remove.
RAE · Zheng et al. · NYU · 2025.10 impact undetermined

RAE: diffuse in a frozen encoder's semantic latent

DiT width ≥ token dim · else it can't fit

Shift by data dim · tokens × channels

Noise-robust decoder · trained on noised latents

1.13
FID · guided (1.51 unguided)

The latent need not be a reconstruction VAE: semantic latents converge faster once three fixes are in.

RAE, short for representation autoencoder, goes the other way: it replaces the VAE's encoder with a frozen one like DINOv2 and trains only a decoder, which reconstructs as well as the Stable Diffusion VAE or better. These latents hold far more numbers per token, so diffusion on them needs three fixes: a wider Transformer, a noise shift that grows with the latent's size, and a decoder trained to handle noisy latents. With those in place, training converges much faster, as the curves on the right show.
JiT · Just image Transformers · Li & He · 2025.11 impact undetermined

JiT: skip the latent, predict clean pixels

Plain ViT on raw pixels: one 32×32×3 patch is 3072-dim.

JiT argues: clean images lie on a low-dim manifold, noise does not; so predict x, and a plain ViT works on pixels.

JiT, short for Just image Transformers, makes the opposite bet: no latent at all, just raw pixels. The argument: clean images lie on a thin, low-dimensional surface in pixel space, but noise and velocity do not, so predict the clean image. In the toy on the left, a two-dimensional spiral is hidden in a high-dimensional space, and only predicting the clean data recovers it. So a plain Vision Transformer can work on large pixel patches: a clean patch has simple structure, while its noise is thousands of independent random values, far harder to output. So JiT needs no autoencoder, no pretrained encoder and no extra loss.
Chapter 5 · summary

The 2025 default: latent + DiT + rectified flow + LLM

BackboneU-Net→DiT→MMDiT · single-stream2022 → 2024
Objectiveε-prediction→velocity (FM / RF)→+ logit-normal + shift2022 → 2024
Text conditioningcross-attn · CLIP→joint attn · T5→LLM / VLM encoder2022 → 2025
Open weightsSDXL→FLUX.1→Qwen-Image · FLUX.2 · Z-Image2023 → 2025
Latentreconstruction VAE→REPA · VA-VAE · REPA-E→RAE (semantic) vs JiT (pixels)open in 2026

A better recipe, not a new model family; still tens of ODE steps per image, which chapter 6 attacks.

To sum up, five parts of the recipe changed. The backbone went from U-Net to Transformer, mostly in the MMDiT style. The objective moved to velocity, with the middle noise levels trained most and a shift toward more noise at high resolution. SD3 marked that switch, though underneath it is still diffusion. Text conditioning went from CLIP and cross-attention to T5 and joint attention, then to large language models. The leading open model went from SDXL to FLUX.1, then to newer models such as Qwen-Image, FLUX.2 and Z-Image. And the latent space became a design target: REPA links diffusion to a pretrained image encoder, RAE uses that encoder's features as the latent, and JiT drops the latent for raw pixels. Which way wins remains an open question in 2026. Still, all of these models need tens of network calls per image.

Chapter 6 · 2020 → 2026

From 1000 steps
to one

A · ODE solvers B · reflow (straighter paths) C · progressive distillation C · Consistency Models D · ADD · SDXL Turbo D · DMD C · MeanFlow

Four routes: A solvers · B straighter paths · C learn to jump · D match distributions

Next: speed, and how we got from a thousand network calls per image down to one. Each call runs the whole network, one after another, so the real question is how few calls we can get away with. People have found four routes, and each tag shows its route letter. Route A uses a better ODE solver, a smarter numerical method for following the deterministic path from noise to image. It needs no training, but it stalls around ten steps. Route B straightens the paths with reflow, which retrains the model on noise and image pairs it generated itself. Route C learns to jump over many steps at once. It began with distillation: the slow model acts as a teacher, and a fast student learns to match it in far fewer steps. Route D only asks the student to produce the same distribution of images as the teacher, not to follow the same path.
Acceleration · network calls per image

Five years, 1000× fewer network calls

Solvers stall near 10 steps; getting to 1 step meant training a new network.

Here is the progress in one chart: network calls per sample, on a log scale. The top three bars need no extra training. Better solvers cut DDPM's thousand steps to a few dozen, then to about ten. Below about ten steps they break down, because the paths are curved. Everything at four steps or fewer needs extra training: first four steps, then one, and eventually one step with no teacher at all. SDXL Turbo brought one step to text-to-image. DMD2's one-step student even beat its many-step teacher. And MeanFlow got to one step while training from scratch. In five years, a thousand calls became one.
Route A · better solvers · 2020 → 2023

Smarter integrators: 1000 steps to 10–20

DDIM · predict clean, re-noise to next level$$x_s=\alpha_s\,\hat x_0(x_t)+\sigma_s\,\hat\epsilon(x_t)$$

DPM-Solver++ · stable at high CFG
EDM · Heun, 35 NFE
UniPC · Wan2.1 default

below ~10 steps: curved paths → blur

Same network, better integrator: no retraining, but curved paths cap it near 10 steps.

Route A first. The network stays the same. Only the way we step along the path changes. DDIM, in the box on the right, is the template for everything that follows: predict the clean image, then add back just enough noise to land on the next, cleaner noise level. DPM-Solver computes part of the path exactly and only approximates the part that depends on the network, which gives good images in about ten calls. DPM-Solver++ works with the predicted clean image, which keeps it stable under strong guidance. UniPC, a later solver in the same family, is still the default in the open video model Wan. But no solver gets far below ten steps: the path curves, and big steps blur the image.
Route C begins · learn to jump · Salimans & Ho · 2022.02

Distill two teacher steps into one, repeat

8192 → 4
steps, halved each round
4-step FID 3.0 · CIFAR-10
recall primer · v-prediction, born here$$v=\alpha_t\,\epsilon-\sigma_t\,x$$

v adopted: SD 2.x 768, Imagen Video
Guided distillation (2022.10) bakes CFG into one pass
FLUX.1 [dev]: “guidance distillation” details undisclosed

Each round halves the step count, but every round retrains the student.

Route C starts with distillation. An early attempt trained a one-step student directly on the teacher's samples, with blurry results. Progressive distillation, in 2022, takes smaller bites. The student matches two teacher steps with one of its own, then becomes the next teacher, as the figure shows. Halving again and again went from about eight thousand steps to four, but every round means training a new student. It also introduced v-prediction, where the network outputs a velocity, a mix of noise and clean image that stays stable with few steps. Guidance distillation, which came up briefly earlier, then folds the two passes of classifier-free guidance, with and without the prompt, into one network. FLUX.1 dev, for example, was trained with guidance distillation.
Route C · learn to jump · Consistency Models · OpenAI · 2023.03

Learn the trajectory's endpoint, not its tangent

same output along a path · identity at the start$$f_\theta(x_t,t)=f_\theta(x_{t'},t'),\quad f_\theta(x,t_{\min})=x$$

CD (distillation): teacher takes one ODE step
CT (training): no teacher

One network call maps any noisy point on a trajectory directly to its clean endpoint.

Next: consistency models, from OpenAI in 2023. A diffusion network learns the tangent of the path, which way to move next. A consistency model learns where the path ends. From any point on a path, it outputs the same clean endpoint, as the animation shows, so one call is enough. At the lowest noise level, it simply returns its input, which anchors every path to a clean image. Training needs only neighbouring points on a path. In consistency distillation, a teacher's solver step finds the neighbour. In consistency training, both come from the same image and noise, with no teacher. The loss makes the two answers agree, and that agreement spreads along the whole path. With distillation, a single call already gave convincing images.
Route C · consistency follow-ups · 2023 → 2024

Teacher-free CT beat distillation; LCM went plug-in

2.51
1-step FID · CIFAR-10
iCT, no teacher

LCM / LCM-LoRA
SD in 2–4 steps after 32 A100 hours

DALL·E 3 decoder: CD-distilled to 2 steps

Training without a teacher soon beat distillation, and a plug-in LoRA let Stable Diffusion sample in 2–4 steps.

Consistency models had three follow-ups. First, in late 2023, a better loss and training schedule made consistency training, with no teacher, actually beat distillation. Second, latent consistency models, or LCM, cheaply distilled Stable Diffusion in its latent space down to two to four steps. Their LoRA version plugs into fine-tuned Stable Diffusion and SDXL models without retraining. In the figure, a style LoRA alone, in the top row, looks unfinished after a few steps. With LCM-LoRA added, in the bottom row, it looks done. Third, DALL·E 3 used consistency distillation to cut its image decoder, the diffusion model that turns latents back into pixels, to two steps.
Route D · match distributions · ADD · Stability AI · 2023.11

A teacher plus a discriminator train a one-step student

50 → 1
steps · SDXL Turbo
per Stability
207 ms
512² image · A100
per Stability

Blind test: 1 step beats 4-step LCM-XL; 4 steps beat 50-step SDXL

Sharp one-step images came from matching the output distribution, not the teacher's path.

Now route D. Adversarial diffusion distillation, or ADD, arrived with SDXL Turbo in November 2023. The student starts from SDXL and trains with two losses. One is adversarial, as in a GAN: a discriminator learns to tell real images from the student's, and the student learns to fool it. The other is score distillation: add noise to the student's output, let the frozen teacher denoise it, and pull the student toward that result. Fifty steps became one, fast enough for real time. In blind tests, people preferred its single step to four steps of LCM. The strip at the bottom shows LCM at one, two and four steps, then ADD's single step, already sharp. That sharpness comes from the discriminator, which only judges whether an image looks real.
Route D · DMD · Yin et al. · MIT / Adobe · 2023.11

One step or many? Hard to tell

By late 2023, one network call could pass for a multi-step Stable Diffusion image.

Before we look inside DMD, short for distribution matching distillation, a quick quiz. Each column pairs a many-step Stable Diffusion image with one from DMD's one-step student, distilled from it. Try to guess which one is the one-step image. [click] The red boxes mark the one-step images: bottom, top, bottom, bottom, top. If some were hard to call, that is the point. By late 2023, one network call could pass for the many-step teacher.
Route D · match distributions · DMD · MIT / Adobe · 2023.11

Real score minus fake score is the gradient

reverse KL · scores on re-noised generator output$$\nabla_\theta D_{KL}\approx\mathbb{E}_{z,t}\Big[-\big(s_{\text{real}}(x_t,t)-s_{\text{fake}}(x_t,t)\big)\tfrac{\partial G_\theta(z)}{\partial\theta}\Big]$$
2.62
1-step FID
ImageNet 64
11.49
FID · zero-shot
COCO-30k

Distribution matching now powers Turbo products and real-time video (Self-Forcing, ch8)

The teacher says where real images are dense; a second network tracks where the student over-clusters.

So how does DMD work? It drops the idea that each noise sample must map to one particular teacher image. The one-step generator starts as a copy of the teacher and only has to match the teacher's distribution of images. It minimizes a KL divergence, a standard distance between distributions, measured on noisy versions of its outputs. The gradient needs just two scores, which, remember, point toward more likely images. The real score comes from the frozen teacher and points to where real images are. The fake score comes from a second diffusion model, trained on the student's samples, and points to where the student's images pile up. Their difference pushes samples toward real data and away from crowded spots. On its own this tends to collapse onto a few kinds of images, so DMD adds a small regression loss: for a fixed set of noise inputs, the student must also reproduce the teacher's images. Real score minus fake score: that is the whole trick.
Route D · DMD2 · LADD · 2024 → 2025

Turbo products run on distribution matching

1.28
1-step FID · ImageNet 64
DMD2 beats its teacher
SD3-Turbo · LADD · 4 steps FLUX.1 [schnell] · 1–4 steps SDXL-Lightning Z-Image-Turbo · 8 NFE

Real-time video: CausVid, Self-Forcing → ch8

Matching the output distribution, not the teacher's path, became the main recipe for 1–4-step products.

In 2024, DMD2 dropped that regression loss and its costly teacher pairs. It stays stable by updating the fake score more often and adding a discriminator trained on real images. Because it sees real data, the student can even beat its teacher. These are its four-step SDXL images. Distribution matching now powers the Turbo versions of many image models, and later it made real-time video possible.
Route C · MeanFlow · Geng et al. · CMU / MIT · 2025.05

Learn the average velocity, jump in one step

average velocity over an interval$$u(z_t,r,t)=\frac{1}{t-r}\int_r^t v(z_\tau,\tau)\,d\tau$$
MeanFlow identity · one JVP$$u=v-(t-r)\,\tfrac{d}{dt}u$$

Learn the average velocity over a whole interval, and one big jump replaces many small steps.

Back to route C: MeanFlow, from 2025. Flow matching predicts a velocity, the direction of motion at one point. MeanFlow learns the average velocity over a whole interval: the chord, the straight line between the interval's two ends, not the tangent. Then one jump covers the whole interval, and an interval from pure noise to data is one-step generation. The average is an integral, so it can't be supervised directly. The identity in the highlighted box rewrites it as the ordinary velocity minus a correction term, which costs one extra derivative pass. When the interval shrinks to zero, this is plain flow matching. As the interval widens, the amber step along the tangent drifts off the curve, while the chord still lands on it.
