From-scratch one-step models sharply narrowed the gap on ImageNet; replacing distillation is open.

These ImageNet models were trained from scratch, with no teacher. With one call, MeanFlow beat every earlier one-step model trained from scratch, and two calls did better still. Guidance is built into the training target, so even one step is guided. Follow-ups have improved it further, one even working directly on pixels. One step no longer needs a teacher.
Chapter 6 · summary

Four routes, two concept shifts

A · SolversDDIM→DPM-Solver++ · EDM→UniPC2020 → 2023
B · Straighter pathsreflow (2-rectified flow)→InstaFlow2022 → 2023
C · Learn to jumpPD→CM · LCM→iCT→MeanFlow2022 → 2025
D · Match distributionsADD · DMD→DMD2 · LADD→Turbo products2023 → 2025
DivergenceCM: diverse, soft+DMD: sharp, collapse-prone→rCM: both, 14B2025

Learn the jump, not the tangent; match the distribution, not the path.

Here are the four routes side by side. Solvers took a thousand steps to ten or twenty with no training, and they remain standard. Reflow straightens the paths, but plain flow-matching models like SD3 or FLUX still need tens of steps. Learning to jump moved from distilling a teacher to training from scratch. Distribution matching is the main recipe for products that sample in one to four steps. Underneath, two ideas changed: learn where the path ends, not just which way it points, and match the distribution of images instead of copying each path. Consistency methods tend to be diverse but soft, and DMD sharp but prone to collapse. In 2025, a method called rCM combined the two. For video, where each call costs far more, these speed-ups matter even more.
Video: OpenAI, Sora (2024) · generated, not a drone shot
07
Chapter 7 · 2022 → 2024

From image models to spacetime patches

VDM · factorized 3D U-Net Video LDM · temporal layers Sora · spacetime-patch DiT Movie Gen · 30B HunyuanVideo · open weights
Next: video. Time adds an axis that multiplies compute and memory, and captioned video is far scarcer than captioned images. In two years, video diffusion went through three architectures. In 2022, VDM, short for video diffusion models, stretched the image U-Net to video, with separate layers for space and time, working in pixels. In 2023, Video LDM froze Stable Diffusion and trained only new temporal layers, which mix information across frames. In February 2024, Sora's report described a diffusion Transformer over spacetime patches, small blocks of compressed video that span a few frames. By the end of 2024, Movie Gen and HunyuanVideo wrote down the full recipe: a 3D VAE that compresses time as well as space, flow matching, rewritten captions, and a Transformer with full attention, where every patch attends to every other patch.
Three regimes · 2022 → 2025

Video diffusion changed architecture twice in two years

Each switch answered one question: how to afford the extra time axis.

The timeline places each model at its first public release. Pixel-space cascades came first, from VDM in 2022 to Imagen Video, chaining models that raise the resolution stage by stage. Latent U-Nets with temporal layers defined 2023, from Video LDM to Stable Video Diffusion. After Sora in 2024, Transformers on spacetime patches took over, and CogVideoX, Movie Gen and HunyuanVideo published the recipe. The grey lane is a different route: turn video into discrete tokens, like words, and generate them one after another, each conditioned on the ones before. That is called autoregressive generation. It fell behind diffusion on quality, but it gave video models the causal video tokenizer, which encodes each frame using only earlier frames. In late 2025 this route came back with InfinityStar, a video model from the Infinity family, built on VAR, short for visual autoregressive modeling. Instead of one token at a time, it builds each short clip coarse to fine, predicting each sharper scale from the coarser ones, and generates the clips one after another.
Video Diffusion Models · Ho et al. · Google · 2022.04

VDM: inflate the image U-Net, factorize space and time

Joint image–video training: extra images ride along as frames; their temporal attention is masked to identity.

Two VDM defaults: separate space/time layers (until Sora-era full attention) and joint image-video training.

VDM, from Google in 2022, was among the first to show that diffusion works for video. It inflates the image U-Net to take a stack of frames, but its convolutions still look only within each frame. Attention is factorized, as the diagram shows: spatial attention inside each frame, then temporal attention along time, linking the same position across frames. That costs little more than running the image model on each frame. With temporal attention switched off, it is an image model, so VDM trained on images and videos together. Both habits stayed standard for two years.
VDM · extending fixed-length clips

Extending a clip needs reconstruction guidance

each step: correct the prediction for new frames b so the reconstruction of known frames a matches them$\tilde{x}^b=\hat{x}^b-\frac{w_r\alpha_t}{2}\,\nabla_{z^b_t}\big\lVert x^a-\hat{x}^a(z_t)\big\rVert^2,\quad w_r>1$

Pasting in known frames fails; steering the model's own reconstruction toward them gives coherent extensions.

VDM makes clips of a fixed length. To extend one, the new frames must continue the known ones. The simple approach pastes a noisy copy of the known frames into the sample at every step, and it fails: on the left, where each row is one sample, the new frames drift away. Reconstruction guidance instead nudges the new frames at every step, so that the model's prediction of the known frames matches the real ones. On the right, the extensions stay coherent. In short, don't paste the known frames in. Steer the model toward them.
Video LDM · Align your Latents · NVIDIA · 2023.04

Freeze Stable Diffusion, train only temporal layers

learned mix with the frozen image layer$z \leftarrow \alpha\,z+(1-\alpha)\,l_\phi(z)$
$l_\phi$: new temporal layer · $\alpha$ learned; $\alpha=1$ is the image model
512×1024 driving T2V up to 1280×2048 transfers to DreamBooth models

Images teach appearance, scarce video teaches only motion: the 2023 template behind AnimateDiff and SVD.

Video LDM, from NVIDIA in 2023, asked: can a strong text-to-image model simply be taught time? Freeze Stable Diffusion, insert new temporal layers, and train only those, on video. A learned weight blends each frozen layer with its temporal partner, and when it is set fully to the image side, the network is exactly the image model. The animation on the left shows the idea: independent frames get aligned into one clip, hence the title, Align your Latents. The decoder also gets temporal layers, to stop flicker. The temporal layers can even be plugged into DreamBooth versions of Stable Diffusion to animate them, an idea AnimateDiff later built on. Images teach appearance, so video only has to teach motion.
Sora · OpenAI · 2024.02 · report, no paper

Sora: minute-long video from a diffusion transformer

~1 min
longest video
2048²
images, same model
1920×1080 ↔ 1080×1920
native aspect ratios
objective · size · data · compute undisclosed

Before 2024: inflated image U-Nets, few-second clips, square training crops

Known parts, combined and trained at scale, gave minute-long coherent video in 2024; the details stayed secret.

Then, in February 2024, came Sora. The samples were a shock: up to a minute long, with scenes that keep their 3D shape as the camera moves, in any format from widescreen to portrait. The same model makes images, animates stills, extends clips and blends videos. None of the pieces was new: latent diffusion, a diffusion Transformer, patches and recaptioning. What was new was the combination, trained at very large scale on videos kept at their native size and shape.
Sora · what the report discloses

Video as one sequence of spacetime patches

token count · latent T×H×W$N=\frac{T}{p_t}\cdot\frac{H}{p_h}\cdot\frac{W}{p_w}$
$p_t,p_h,p_w$: patch size per axis · cost $\propto N^2$
image = 1-frame video
undisclosed: compression, patch size, objective, params, data

Open recipe (Movie Gen, HunyuanVideo):
3D VAE + full-attention DiT + flow matching

Patches turn any size, length or aspect ratio into one token sequence for a diffusion Transformer.

So how does Sora work? Here is the outline OpenAI gave. A compression network maps the video into a latent that is smaller in time and space. The latent is cut into spacetime patches that act like tokens in a language model. An image is simply a video with one frame, so the same model handles both. Arranging noise patches in a grid of any size sets the resolution, duration and aspect ratio. A text-conditioned diffusion Transformer turns noisy patches into clean ones, as the animation walks through. With full attention, every token attends to every other, so the cost grows with the square of the token count. That is why compressing the video hard before cutting it into patches matters so much.
Sora · native-size training · compute

Train at native size, sample any shape

mixed-size batching undisclosed

No cropping: native aspect ratios frame subjects better, and a fixed seed keeps improving with compute.

Sora's second ingredient was training at native size. At the top, one model makes vertical, square and widescreen video, where earlier systems trained only on square clips. On the bottom left, a model trained on squares can cut the subject out of the frame, while native training frames it properly. On the bottom right, the same seed keeps getting better with more and more training compute.
Sora · claimed emergent abilities

“World simulator”: emergent, but brittle

“scaling video generation models is a promising path towards building general purpose simulators of the physical world”

qualitative claims · no metrics

Scale bought surprising consistency, but the report's own failures show physics is not reliably learned.

OpenAI also pointed to abilities that nobody built in, which seem to emerge from scale. The scene keeps its 3D shape as the camera moves. Objects persist: the dog stays put while people pass in front of it. Simple interactions work: a bite leaves a mark on the burger. And prompted with Minecraft, it renders the game world. Hence the quote at the bottom right: scaling video models may lead to simulators of the physical world. But the red-tagged clip shows the limit: shattering glass behaves wrongly. Scale bought consistency, not reliable physics.
Factorized vs full attention · 2022 → 2024

Factorized attention misses large motion

attention cost per layer$\underbrace{T(HW)^2+HW\,T^2}_{\text{factorized}}\ \ll\ \underbrace{(THW)^2}_{\text{full}}$

~73K tokens: Movie Gen, 16 s at 768², after a 3D VAE (compresses time too) + patchify

Full attention became affordable once 3D VAEs and patches cut clips to tens of thousands of tokens.

Why did factorized attention last two years, and why did it end? Remember, its temporal layers only link the same position across frames. On the left, a man moves between frames, so the patches covering him never attend to each other directly, and large motion becomes inconsistent. The ball on the right shows the same: the factorized link points to where the ball was, while full 3D attention follows it. Full attention is expensive, but it became affordable in 2024 because 3D VAEs and patches cut a clip to tens of thousands of tokens, and the long-sequence tools built for language models could be reused.
Movie Gen · Meta · 2024.10

Movie Gen: LLaMa3 blocks + flow matching at 30B

frames × height × width tokens$\tfrac{256}{8}\times\tfrac{768}{16}\times\tfrac{768}{16}=73{,}728$
16 s · 768² · TAE 8×8×8 · patch 1×2×2
flow matching > v-pred + zero SNR
(their ablation) → 1080p upsampler Audio 13B · 48 kHz no weights

The most complete recipe a frontier lab published in 2024: choices ablated, written down, LLM tools reused.

In October 2024, Meta published Movie Gen, the most complete video recipe any frontier lab wrote down that year. Its autoencoder compresses time as well as space. The backbone stays deliberately plain: it reuses the blocks of Meta's language model, Llama 3, so the scaling tools built for language models carry over. In their tests, flow matching beat v-prediction. Three text encoders read the prompt, and a video version of Llama writes the training captions. The main model has thirty billion parameters, and a separate model adds sound.
HunyuanVideo · Tencent · 2024.12 · open weights

HunyuanVideo: the recipe with open weights

13B+
largest open video model then
4×8×8
causal 3D VAE · 16 ch
dual → single stream MLLM text encoder + CLIP-L flow matching · 3D RoPE

Near-frontier quality with open weights made the 2024 recipe a shared research platform.

In December 2024, Tencent released HunyuanVideo, with code and weights from day one. With over 13 billion parameters, it was the largest open video model at the time, and in its own professional human evaluation it beat Runway Gen-3, Luma 1.6 and three leading Chinese models. The recipe is close to Movie Gen's. Its 3D VAE is causal, so the first frame is encoded on its own and an image is just a one-frame video. And its blocks process text and video separately before joining them, as in FLUX. Open weights brought a wave of LoRAs and image-to-video extensions, and the recipe became a shared research platform.
Recap · VDM → HunyuanVideo

Five choices, one converged recipe

Latentpixels→per-frame 2D VAE→3D VAE · causal 4×8×8 / TAE 8×8×8VDM → CogVideoX
Backbonefactorized 3D U-Net→frozen SD + temporal layers→full-attention TransformerVDM → CogVideoX
Objectiveε (some v)→SD objective→v-pred + zero SNR→flow matchingVDM → Movie Gen
Text encoderBERT→CLIP→T5→UL2 + ByT5 + MetaCLIP · MLLM + CLIP-LVDM → HunyuanVideo
Captionspaired captions→recaptioning + GPT prompt expansion→VLM captioners · LLaMa3-VideoSora → Movie Gen

By end-2024 video diffusion meant 3D VAE + full-attention Transformer + flow matching + LLM-grade text.

To sum up video so far, here are five design choices. Read each row from left to right. The latent went from pixels, to per-frame latents, to 3D VAEs. The backbone went from a factorized U-Net, to frozen Stable Diffusion with temporal layers, to full-attention Transformers. The objective went from predicting noise, through v-prediction, to flow matching. Text encoders went from BERT and CLIP to T5 and then language models, and machine-written captions became part of the recipe. By the end of 2024, that was the recipe, and everything that follows starts from it.

08
Chapter 8 · 2024 → 2026

Video becomes real-time, audible, interactive

Wan · open base Diffusion Forcing CausVid → Self Forcing Veo 3 · native audio Genie 3 · world models zero-shot reasoners omni models
Next: what happened to video after that recipe. In 2024, a video model still denoised one fixed-length, silent clip, all at once. Over the next two years, that changed in four directions. First, Alibaba released Wan, a strong video model with open weights that anyone can download and build on. Second, video became real-time: frames appear one after another, like a live stream. Third, Veo 3 generated sound together with the picture. And fourth, Genie 3 turned video models into interactive worlds.
Wan 2.1 · Alibaba Tongyi · 2025.02

Wan made a strong video base fully open

  • Open: Apache 2.0 weights + code
  • Wan-VAE: causal 3D, 4×8×8 compression
  • 1.3B needs ~8.19 GB VRAM: 5 s of 480p in ~4 min on an RTX 4090

Strong, free and runnable on one gaming GPU: arguably the shared starting point for video research.

Wan, from Alibaba, did not introduce a new idea. It took the standard recipe, a diffusion Transformer trained with flow matching on compressed video, engineered it carefully, and in early 2025 released weights and code under a permissive license. Its autoencoder is causal: it encodes each chunk of video from that chunk and earlier frames only, so it can compress and rebuild videos of any length, piece by piece. The small version runs on a single gaming graphics card, putting a strong video model within reach of almost any lab. It can also write Chinese and English text inside the video, as you can see in the samples on the left.
Wan ecosystem · 2025 → 2026

Most open work in this chapter is built on Wan

One reading: research moved from “train a base first” to “post-train an open base”, as with Stable Diffusion.

Wan quickly became the base for much of the open work on video. Self Forcing, one of the real-time methods coming up next, starts from Wan, and so do an audio and video model and several world models. By April 2025, Wan had been downloaded millions of times. Wan 2.2, shown at the bottom, uses two expert networks: one handles the early, very noisy steps, and the other takes over for the later, cleaner ones. Why split the work by noise level? Because early steps lay out the scene and late steps refine the details, which are different jobs. Only one expert runs per step, so each step stays cheap. The price is storing two sets of weights.
Diffusion Forcing · Chen et al. · 2024.07

Give every frame its own noise level

Next-frame prediction and full-sequence diffusion are two noise patterns; Diffusion Forcing trains on all of them.

Now to real-time video. There are two classic ways to generate a sequence. The first is autoregressive: generate one frame at a time, each conditioned on the previous ones. In training, the model is given the real previous frames, which is called teacher forcing. It can stream, but small errors pile up, and long videos drift away. The second is full-sequence diffusion: all frames share one noise level and are denoised together. Quality is high, but the length is fixed and nothing streams. Diffusion Forcing combines the two. In training, every frame gets its own random noise level, so a model that looks only at earlier frames learns to denoise any mix of a cleaner past and a noisier future. In the animation, the top row denoises everything together, the middle row finishes frames one by one, and the bottom row is a diagonal wave, one of many schedules the same model can follow. So next-frame prediction and full-sequence diffusion are just two noise patterns, and Diffusion Forcing trains on all of them.
Diffusion Forcing · Chen et al. · 2024.07

Slightly noisy history keeps rollouts stable

one noise level per frame$$\mathcal L=\mathop{\mathbb E}\limits_{k_t\sim\mathcal U\{0..K\}\ \text{iid}}\sum_t\big\|\epsilon_t-\epsilon_\theta\big(x_1^{k_1},\dots,x_t^{k_t};\,k_{1:t}\big)\big\|^2$$

Frame $t$ is noised to its own random level $k_t$; a causal net denoises every mix and is told every level $k_{1:t}$.

Teacher forcing: clean past, noisy present. Full-sequence: one shared level.

Train the model to expect an imperfect past, and its own mistakes stop snowballing.

The loss on the right is ordinary denoising, except that each frame has its own noise level, and the network only looks back in time. The benefit shows in the video. Since the model has seen noisy pasts, you can keep its history slightly noisy, so it does not over-trust its own imperfect frames. Diffusion Forcing, on top, then stays stable far beyond the training length, while full-sequence diffusion, in the middle, loses consistency, and teacher forcing, at the bottom, falls apart. Train the model to expect an imperfect past, and its mistakes stop snowballing.
Causal video diffusion · 2024 → 2025

To stream video, a frame may only look back

Diffusion Forcing (Chen et al. 2024): train each frame at its own noise level, so the past can be partly noisy.

A bidirectional model shows nothing until every frame is done; a causal one can show frames as they come.

So how does a model stream? In these attention masks, each row is a frame, and the coloured cells are the frames it may look at. In a bidirectional DiT, on the left, every frame attends to every other frame, so all frames are denoised together and you see nothing until the whole clip is finished. With a causal mask, in the middle, a frame sees only itself and earlier frames, so it can be shown as soon as it is done. Past frames never change, so their keys and values are computed once and kept in a KV cache. Block-causal attention, on the right, is a compromise: frames inside a chunk see each other freely, and across chunks they only look back. The catch: causal models trained from scratch were clearly worse than bidirectional ones. So Diffusion Forcing made causal video diffusion stable, but it was still slow, and its quality still lagged behind.
CausVid · Yin et al. · 2024.12

A bidirectional teacher trains a fast causal student

219 s → 1.3 s
teacher, 128 frames →
student's first frame
9.4 FPS
streaming after that, one GPU
  • block-causal attention + KV cache (past frames not recomputed)
  • DMD: 50 → 4 steps
  • student initialized on teacher ODE pairs

Asymmetric distillation: a teacher that sees the future grades a student that never does.

CausVid's answer: start from a strong bidirectional model and convert it into a causal one. The original model stays bidirectional and becomes the teacher. The student gets block-causal attention and a KV cache, and is trained with DMD, the distribution-matching method we saw earlier. Fifty steps become four. The result: you see the first frame almost at once, instead of after minutes, and the rest of the video then streams on a single GPU. But how can a bidirectional teacher teach a causal student? Distribution matching only asks that the student's whole videos look like the teacher's, never that it copy the teacher frame by frame. So a teacher that sees the future can grade a student that never does.
Self Forcing · Huang et al. · 2025.06

Train on your own rollouts to close the train–test gap

video-level distribution matching$\displaystyle\min_\theta\ \mathcal D\Big(\textstyle\prod_i p_\theta(x_i\mid \hat x_{<i})\ \Big\|\ p_{\text{data}}(x_{1:N})\Big)$

via DMD; the teacher stands in for real data

(a) real past · (b) noisy real past · (c) past = its own samples, as at test time

Like learning to drive by driving yourself, with the instructor grading the whole trip, not each turn.

One problem remained, a classic one called exposure bias, and Self Forcing went after it. In training, the model sees real past frames, but at test time it sees its own imperfect ones, and that mismatch makes errors snowball. The figure shows three ways to train: teacher forcing on real past frames, Diffusion Forcing on noisy real frames, and, on the right, Self Forcing on the model's own samples, as at test time. So in training, the model generates a whole clip by itself, frame by frame with its KV cache, and a distribution-matching loss compares the whole video against the teacher. This stays cheap: the student needs only a few steps, and gradients flow only through the last denoising step. It is like learning to drive by driving, with the instructor grading the whole trip, not each turn.
Self Forcing · Huang et al. · 2025.06

A post-training recipe: an open bidirectional base can cheaply be made causal, few-step and much faster.

Here is one prompt from three models: bidirectional Wan on the left, CausVid in the middle, and Self Forcing on the right. Self Forcing streams in real time on one GPU, with the first frame in well under a second. Its quality matches the bidirectional model it started from, yet you start watching almost immediately. And converting the open model takes only a short training run. It turned offline rendering into a live stream and started follow-ups, like LongLive and Self-Forcing++, that stretch videos to several minutes.
Veo 3 · Google DeepMind · 2025.05

Video generation leaves the silent era

“We’re emerging from the silent era of video generation.”
— Demis Hassabis, Google I/O 2025
target$$p(z^{v}\mid c)\ \longrightarrow\ p(z^{v},z^{a}\mid c)$$

audio + video latents, diffused jointly by a transformer

coupling & scale undisclosed

One prompt now yields picture, ambience, effects and lip-synced dialogue together, not dubbed later.

That clip came from Veo 3, announced by Google in May 2025: the dialogue, the sound effects and the ambience were all generated together with the picture. Under the hood it is latent diffusion: audio and video each have their own autoencoder, and a Transformer denoises both sets of latents together. As the equation on the right says, the model now learns video and audio jointly, given the prompt. Before, a separate model added sound afterwards, which made lip-sync hard. Generating both together keeps them aligned. By 2026, native audio, meaning sound generated with the picture, is standard in flagship video models.
Ovi · LTX-2 · 2025 → 2026

Open models show one way to fuse audio and video

Two towers that talk through cross-attention: a public recipe, not a description of Veo 3.

Two open models show one way to build this. Ovi, on the left, has two identical Transformer towers: one for video, started from Wan, and one for audio, trained from scratch. In every block, the towers exchange information through cross-attention in both directions, with positions rescaled so that the same moment lines up in audio and video. LTX-2, on the right, does the same with a large video stream and a smaller audio stream. So the open recipe is two towers that keep talking to each other.
Genie 3 · Google DeepMind · 2025.08

A playable world, generated frame by frame

Arguably a game engine without a game engine: no stored geometry, each frame imagined from history + actions.

The fourth direction is interactivity. In August 2025, Google DeepMind showed Genie 3, a world model: it generates a world you can move through, responding to your actions. Earlier systems had limits. GameNGen ran Doom in real time, but only that game. Oasis generated Minecraft, but scenes changed when you looked away. And Genie 2's worlds lasted only a short while. Genie 3 builds worlds from text in real time and keeps them mostly consistent for minutes. On the left, a prompt adds an event while you explore. On the right, paint stays on the wall after the camera looks away and back. Each frame is generated from the history so far and the user's latest action, with no stored 3D geometry, so the consistency is learned. It is a game engine without a game engine.
World models · 2024 → 2026

From one game to any world, in real time

Open real-time world models followed within months, and several reuse the Self Forcing recipe.

This timeline shows how fast it moved, with Google on top and everyone else below. In the clips underneath, GameNGen runs Doom, while Matrix-Game 2.0 and Tencent's HY-World 1.5 let you steer through a generated world in real time. Genie 3 was the step from one game to any world you can describe. Google followed in early 2026 with Project Genie, which lets users explore such worlds, and with a Waymo world model for driving simulation, built on Genie 3. Open followers came within months, often reusing what we just saw: Matrix-Game 2.0 uses Self Forcing, LingBot-World builds on Wan, and Waypoint-1 combines Diffusion Forcing with Self Forcing. The open problem is memory: these models see only recent frames, so anything older must be stored and retrieved explicitly.
Video reasoners · Wiedemer et al. · 2025.09

A video model can solve vision tasks zero-shot

18,384
generated videos ·
62 qualitative + 7 quantitative tasks

Chain-of-frames

frame-by-frame generation as step-by-step visual reasoning

API has an LLM prompt rewriter; specialists still better

One image plus one instruction in, a video out: the answer is in the frames, as with LLM prompting.

Video models may be good for more than videos. Google DeepMind gave Veo 3 one image and a text instruction, and asked it to solve vision tasks zero-shot, meaning with no task-specific training. The four clips show tasks from finding edges to solving a maze. The authors call this chain-of-frames, after chain-of-thought, where a language model writes out its reasoning step by step. Here, each new frame is one more step. And Veo 3 does clearly better than Veo 2, which suggests these skills grow as video models improve. So video models may become general tools for vision, the way language models became general tools for text.

Seedance 2.0: text + image + video + audio in, 4–15 s out

The interface moved from one prompt to any references plus a multi-turn conversation.

By late 2025, the interface itself was changing. Gemini Omni, shown in May 2026, edits video over several turns: a violinist, then the violin made invisible, then a new camera angle. The diagram below shows Kling-Omni, from December 2025. A multimodal language model rewrites the prompt, a diffusion Transformer generates the video, and a final stage upsamples it. Seedance 2.0, from February 2026, takes text, images, video and audio together, including several references at once. So a single prompt has grown into any mix of references plus a multi-turn conversation.

Chapter 9 · 2023 → 2026

Diffusion meets the language model

Diffusion-DPO Flow-GRPO MAR Transfusion GPT-4o image Nano Banana thinking image models beyond vision

Also: image models now post-train like LLMs (DPO → online RL)

Let's go back to images, where after 2023 diffusion began to merge with large language models. This happened in two ways. First, the training recipe: image models learned from human preferences and from reinforcement learning, just as language models do. Second, the architecture: diffusion became one part of a single Transformer that also handles text. And in 2025 the flagship products moved inside chat models, with GPT-4o image generation and Nano Banana.
Diffusion-DPO · Wallace et al. · 2023.11

Align to human taste without a reward model

Diffusion-DPO loss (simplified)$$\Delta(x)=\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t)\|^2-\|\epsilon-\epsilon_{\text{ref}}(x_t)\|^2$$$$\mathcal L=-\log\sigma\big(-\beta\,[\Delta(x^{w})-\Delta(x^{l})]\big)$$

$\Delta$: error vs. frozen reference, pushed lower for winner $x^w$ than loser $x^l$; $\mathbb E_t$, weighting omitted

851K
Pick-a-Pic pairs · SDXL

ReFL · backprop a differentiable reward

DDPO · online RL, any reward

Diffusion-DPO · offline pairs, no sampling

Show which of two images people preferred; the model learns to denoise the winner better.

Language models are tuned with human feedback, where people pick the better of two outputs. For diffusion this was harder, because there was no general scorer for images, and the probability of an image is hard to compute. In 2023, three approaches appeared, shown in the bottom row. ReFL uses a reward model, a network that predicts how much people will like an image, and backpropagates its score into the generator. DDPO treats denoising as a sequence of random decisions and uses reinforcement learning, so the reward can be any black box. Diffusion-DPO, highlighted, needs no reward model at all. It adapts DPO, direct preference optimization, which learns straight from pairs of a preferred and a rejected output. Compared with a frozen copy of the starting model, the denoising error must drop more on the preferred image than on the rejected one. That is the loss on the right. On the left you can see the effect: the tuned model, in the lower row, gives better composition and detail. So why not always backpropagate a reward? Because the reward must be differentiable, and the generator learns to exploit its weak spots, which is called reward hacking.
Flow-GRPO · Liu et al. · 2025.05

An SDE turns flow sampling into a trainable policy

same marginals as the ODE$$dx_t=\Big[v_t(x_t)-\tfrac{1}{2}g_t^2\,\nabla\log p_t(x_t)\Big]dt+g_t\,dw$$$$\hat A_i=\frac{r_i-\mathrm{mean}(\{r_j\})}{\mathrm{std}(\{r_j\})}$$

SD3 convention, $t$: 1→0. $g_t$ ($\sigma_t$ in the figure) sets the injected noise; $g_t=0$ gives back the ODE. Group-relative advantage: no value network.

63→95%
GenEval
59→92%
text rendering (OCR)

Sample several images per prompt, reinforce the above-average ones; deploy with the usual sampler.

Flow models such as SD3 and FLUX sample with the deterministic ODE. Once the starting noise is fixed, there is no randomness to explore, and no probability for each step, which reinforcement learning needs. Flow-GRPO switches to the random, SDE version of the sampler, which produces the same distribution of images and needs no extra network. Now each denoising step adds a little Gaussian noise, so it has a probability, like an action in reinforcement learning. The learning rule, GRPO, short for group relative policy optimization, comes from language models: sample a group of images for each prompt, score them, and reinforce the ones that beat the group average. The rewards are simple checks, such as whether the right objects appear and whether the text is spelled correctly. Both improve a lot, with almost no reward hacking. And the random sampler is only for training. You deploy with the usual one.
Post-training recipe · 2025

Image models now post-train like LLMs

Since: MixGRPO · TempFlow-GRPO · Pref-GRPO · DiffusionNFT

Open image models now follow the LLM recipe: pretrain, fine-tune, learn preferences, then RL online.

The top row is the recipe language models use: pretrain, then supervised fine-tuning, or SFT, on curated examples, then DPO on fixed preference pairs, then online reinforcement learning, where the model is scored on samples it has just generated. Before Flow-GRPO, image models mostly stopped after fine-tuning, because online reinforcement learning looked unstable and expensive. Within months, that changed. Qwen-Image, in August 2025, added DPO and then GRPO. HunyuanImage 3.0, in September, followed the same pattern. And so did Z-Image, in November. So post-training, everything after pretraining, now looks the same for an image generator as for a language model.
MAR · Li et al. · 2024.06

Drop the codebook: a tiny diffusion head per token

Diffusion Loss, per token$$\mathcal L(z,x)=\mathbb E_{\epsilon,t}\big\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t\mid t,z)\big\|^2$$

The transformer gives $z$; a small MLP denoises the continuous token $x$. It replaces the softmax over a VQ codebook.

The transformer decides what comes next; a small diffusion head draws its exact continuous value.

The second thread is the architecture. In 2024, autoregressive image models, which generate an image one piece at a time, came back with VAR, LlamaGen and Chameleon, all using discrete image tokens. But a discrete token is picked from a fixed codebook of image pieces, and that rounding loses information, while diffusion handles continuous values well. MAR keeps the autoregressive Transformer, which outputs a condition vector, z in the figure, for each token. Then, instead of a softmax over the codebook, a tiny diffusion network denoises the continuous token, given that vector. So the Transformer decides what comes next, and diffusion decides exactly what it looks like. Below the equation you can see its samples, each generated from just a class label.
Transfusion · Zhou et al. · Meta · 2024.08

One model predicts text and denoises image patches

one loss, one set of weights$$\mathcal L=\mathcal L_{\text{LM}}+\lambda\,\mathcal L_{\text{DDPM}}$$

cross-entropy on text + noise MSE on VAE-latent patches, $\lambda=5$

at inference

sample text → ⟨BOI⟩ (begin image) → append $n$ noise patches → denoise $T$ steps → ⟨EOI⟩ (end) → back to text

No separate image model: the same weights read the conversation and denoise the picture inside it.

Transfusion goes further: one model that predicts text tokens and generates continuous images, with no discrete image tokens at all. One Transformer reads one mixed sequence of text and image. Text tokens get the usual next-token loss. An image becomes a run of latent patches from the autoencoder, wrapped in begin-of-image and end-of-image markers. The patches are noised, and the model predicts the noise, the plain DDPM loss. Look at the attention mask. It is causal across the sequence, but each image is a filled square, because the patches of one image all see each other. At inference, when it emits the begin-of-image marker, it appends pure-noise patches, denoises them, and then returns to text. How is this different from a language model prompting Stable Diffusion? There, only a prompt passes between two models. Here the same weights read the conversation and denoise the image, with the whole context in view.

This became the blueprint for open unified models, which both understand and generate images, such as JanusFlow, BAGEL and HunyuanImage 3.0.

Meanwhile, the products changed. ChatGPT used to hand a rewritten prompt to a separate diffusion model, DALL·E 3. In March 2025, OpenAI built image generation into GPT-4o itself. In OpenAI's own words, "4o image generation is an autoregressive model natively embedded within ChatGPT." OpenAI credits joint training on images and text, plus heavy post-training, which lets it handle many more objects in one image. The strip at the top shows its signature skill: long, correctly spelled text. So, is diffusion dead? No. Leading models such as Qwen-Image, FLUX.2, Z-Image and Seedream 4.0 still use diffusion or flow matching. The brain moved into the language model, but the pixels are still mostly drawn by diffusion.

As the slider sweeps across this official example, with the instruction "change my shirt color to red and remove earring", the shirt and the earring change, while the face, the pose and the background stay the same. Image models that reason, search, then draw

The goal moved from pretty to correct and readable: plan, look things up, check, then redraw.

Even these models struggled with dense information, such as small text, text in many languages, and precise graphs. They drew in one pass, with no chance to plan or check. Nano Banana Pro, in November 2025, reasons with Gemini before it draws. It can look things up with Google Search, as in this live weather poster, and it renders legible text in many languages, even translating these labels. The chain on the right is the new pattern: reason, search, draw, check, and redraw. Research systems such as GoT and T2I-R1 also let a language model reason before the image is drawn. The goal has moved from pretty pictures to correct ones.
Beyond vision · 2023 → 2025

The same loop now writes text and robot actions

1109
tok/s · Mercury Coder Mini, H100
1479
tok/s · Gemini Diffusion
2146
tok/s · Seed Diffusion, H20
as reported, not like-for-like

For text the “noise” is [MASK]; for robots it is a noisy action sequence. The loop is the same.

Diffusion has also left vision. Text is discrete, so here the noise is masking: each step hides more tokens behind a mask symbol, and the model learns to fill them back in, much like BERT. Methods such as SEDD and MDLM made this competitive with small autoregressive language models. LLaDA scaled it up. On the left, it starts from a fully masked answer and unmasks many tokens in parallel, which is why diffusion language models can be so fast. In robotics, Diffusion Policy, in the middle, denoises a short sequence of future actions from what the camera sees. It can commit to one of several good options, instead of averaging them. So what is diffusion, in the end: a training loss, a renderer for pixels, or a general loop that refines any output step by step?

Trends · 2015 → 2026

Ten trends,
three takeaways

then → now video replays image AR across · diffusion within three takeaways open questions

Nine chapters of milestones, joined into a few lines you can remember.

Let me finish by stepping back. So far we have looked at single papers and systems. Now I'll connect them into a few trends.
Ten trends · 2015 → 2026

Every design choice moved: then → now

Math 1DDPM · score→SDE / ODE→EDM→flow matchingch 1 · 2 · 5
BackboneU-Net→DiT→MMDiTch 5 · 7
Denoise inpixels + cascade→VAE latent→semantic latent or pixels?ch 3 · 5
Text encoderclass label→CLIP→T5→(multimodal) LLMch 3 · 5 · 9
Data 2alt-text pairs→dense recaptionsch 3 · 7
Steps~1000→~50→1–4→real-time videoch 1 · 6 · 8
Controlsampling-time guidance (CFG)→adapters→everything in contextch 2 · 4
Modalityimage→video→interactive worldsch 7 · 8
Post-trainingSFT→DPO→GRPOch 9
vs. autoregression 3rivals→division of labourch 8 · 9

No dedicated slide today: EDM · DreamBooth/LoRA · IP2P/Kontext · REPA/RAE · solvers · VDM/Video LDM · Movie Gen/Hunyuan · DPO/GRPO

Almost every design choice changed; the core idea, learn to undo noise, did not.

Here is the whole talk as one table. Each row is a design choice, from then to now. All of them changed, and the three highlighted rows are my takeaways. The math went from three separate views, the variational, the score and the ODE view, to one framework, with flow matching as the industry default since SD3. Backbones moved from the U-Net to Transformers. Where to denoise, in a latent space or in pixels, is open again. Text encoders grew from class labels to multimodal language models, and better captions often mattered more than a better denoiser. Steps fell from a thousand to just a few, fast enough for real-time video. Control moved from guidance at sampling time, to add-ons like ControlNet and LoRA, and then into the model's context, as extra input tokens. Post-training copied the language-model recipe. And autoregression and diffusion went from rivals to partners. Under every row, models with open weights, from Stable Diffusion to Wan, set what academic researchers can study.
Trend · image → video → worlds

Video replays the image playbook, 7–16 months late

Video borrowed latents, transformers and flow matching from images, then went causal and real-time.

Let me zoom in on one row: video. Video followed the image playbook, half a year to over a year behind. Latents, Transformers and flow matching each worked for images first, in the top row, and reached video later, in the bottom row. Then video left the playbook: Diffusion Forcing, CausVid and Self Forcing made generation causal. Veo 3 added native audio, and GameNGen and Genie 3 made worlds interactive.
Trend · AR + diffusion

AR goes across, diffusion goes within

speaker’s interpretation, not a claim from any paper

One reading: AR orders the pieces; diffusion fills in the continuous values inside each piece.

Here is how I think autoregression and diffusion fit together. Remember MAR's small diffusion head for each token, and Transfusion's two losses, next-token for text and diffusion for images. On the left is Transfusion's attention mask, which is causal across tokens but two-way inside an image. On the right, Self Forcing does the same in time: frames come one after another, and each frame is made by denoising. And diffusion language models fit too: some write text block by block, and fill in the words inside each block by diffusion. So, autoregression handles what goes across: order, meaning and time. Diffusion handles what lies within: the continuous detail inside a token, a frame or a block.
Ten → three

Three trends to take home

One model family; data and conditioning drove the big leaps; diffusion increasingly acts as the renderer.

If you forget everything else, keep three things. One, form: diffusion, score and flow are one object in three coordinate systems, and since SD3, flow matching has been the industrial default. Two, system: many big jumps in prompt following, aesthetics and motion came from data and conditioning, not from the denoiser. Three, role, and this is my reading: the brain is moving into the language model, and diffusion increasingly looks like the high-fidelity renderer, now fast enough for real time.
Open questions · 2026

Four questions still open

Also open: evaluation · cost · copyright

The recipe has converged; its latent, step count, long-range memory and theory have not.

Four questions are still open. First, which latent space: VAE latents, the features of a pretrained encoder as in RAE, or plain pixels as in JiT? JiT's argument is on the left: clean images lie on a thin, low-dimensional surface, and noise does not, so a pixel model should predict the clean image. Which way wins is still undecided. Second, one step: MeanFlow generates good images in a single network call, and a newer method called Drifting reports even better results. Third, memory: Genie 3 stays consistent for minutes, so when you turn back from the desert, the street is still there. Staying consistent much longer, without drift, is open. Fourth, generalization: a model that fit its training data perfectly would only replay training images. Yet two models trained on separate sets of faces, started from the same noise, generate the same new face, so both learned the underlying distribution rather than copying. Exactly why is still open. Also open: evaluation, where arenas are biased, and cost, since frontier video is expensive to serve.
